posts.title: Claude Built a 9.5-Megadalton Protein Shell From Scratch
posts.subtitle: Scientists used an AI agent to design, express, and image a vault particle no cell has ever made.
posts.summary: Anthropic's Science team used Claude as a lab partner to design, express, purify, and image the first engineered vault particles — barrel-shaped protein shells whose biological function has been unknown since their discovery in 1986. The resulting structure, L05, is structurally distinct from the mammalian original, and the project also surfaced concrete failure modes of letting an agent run real wet-lab science.

slides.title: A 1986 Mystery Organelle Gets a Synthetic Twin
slides.body: Vaults are barrel-shaped protein shells about three times the mass of a ribosome, found in nearly every eukaryotic cell since their discovery in 1986 — and nobody knows what they're for. Anthropic's Science team used Claude as a lab partner to build the first engineered versions from scratch.

slides.title: No Natural System to Experiment On
bullets: A mammalian vault is built from 78 copies of one protein (39 per half), with a hollow, barrel-like shape — roughly 67 x 40 nm.
Discovered in 1986 by Rome and Kedersha, who named them for their resemblance to cathedral ceilings under an electron microscope.
Mice without vaults survive fine; proposed roles — nuclear transport, toxin defense, innate immunity — are all unconfirmed.
Without a tunable lab model, there was no way to test structural hypotheses about what vaults actually do.

slides.title: Claude Ran the Discovery-to-Structure Pipeline
bullets: Searched roughly 15 billion predicted proteins and found vault-protein relatives in 29 bacterial phyla and 4 archaeal phyla — under 1% of sequenced species.
Designed DNA constructs and screened 44 candidates in a cell-free system; the best moved into E. coli, where 15 of 24 produced soluble protein.
Proposed a faster purification method: size-exclusion chromatography straight from raw lysate, cutting cells-to-microscopy-grid time from about 3 days to roughly 90 minutes.
Set up and ran cryo-EM reconstruction (RELION) inside an internal multi-agent harness — a first structural model appeared in 34 hours, final maps in about a week.

slides.title: The L05 Vault: Bigger, Fewer Pieces, More Room Inside
slides.body: One phage-derived design, L05, self-assembled into a genuine vault-like shell — and it isn't a scaled copy of the mammalian one.

slides.title: Editing the Cap Taught Them What It's For
bullets: 7 of 15 engineered proteins self-assembled into vault-like particles; cryo-EM confirmed the shape for 4 (2 phage-derived, 2 bacterial).
The cap closes in three tiers, each formed by three protein copies adopting different conformations.
A single point mutation near the cap blocked closure entirely, producing open, rosette-shaped particles — pinpointing that region as the seal.
Duplicating two wall segments (7 to 9 repeats) increased enclosed volume by about 20%, showing the shell's size is a tunable, modular property.

slides.title: Where the Agent Needed a Human Leash
bullets: A Claude-written protocol included an additive that blocked DNA uptake into cells — a mistake that cost the team about two weeks before it was caught.
Early cryo-EM processing skipped a standard mirror-symmetry correction step, quietly blending a structure with its own reflection.
The researchers' response: 'Please let's do normal things unless they don't work' — i.e., don't let the agent improvise past established protocol.
The team reports Claude's reliability improved across newer model versions over the roughly four-month project.

slides.title: What This Actually Proves
bullets: An AI agent can run a real, multi-month structural biology pipeline — sequence search, cloning, expression, purification, cryo-EM, and iterative redesign — with people directing strategy, not pipetting.
The vaults' biological function is still unknown; this didn't solve the 1986 mystery, it built new tools to attack it.
A mystery pocket molecule shaped like coenzyme A turned up inside the L05 structure — unidentified, and possibly a clue to what vaults actually do.
Open question: whether these engineered vaults ever form in their native bacteria or phages — so far they've only been made in E. coli.

questions.prompt: How does the engineered L05 vault's structure compare to the natural mammalian vault, based on the cryo-EM results?
options: It has fewer copies of the vault protein and encloses less volume
It has more copies per half and encloses about 25% more volume despite having fewer wall-repeat units
It is structurally identical to the mammalian vault
It has no cap structure at all
questions.explanation: L05 has 48 copies per half (versus 39 in mammals) and masses about 9.5 megadaltons, enclosing roughly 25% more volume even though its wall is built from fewer repeat units (7 versus 9).

questions.prompt: What specifically went wrong when Claude's cryo-EM workflow processed data without enough oversight?
options: It crashed the lab's compute cluster
It skipped a standard symmetry-correction step, producing a structure blended with its own mirror image
It refused to process the microscopy data
It deleted the raw cryo-EM files
questions.explanation: Skipping a routine step in cryo-EM processing let the reconstruction merge with its own mirror-image conformation — a subtle, specific failure mode rather than a generic 'AI error,' which is why the team pushed back toward standard protocol.

questions.prompt: Which single design change let researchers pinpoint the vault's cap as the structure's sealing mechanism?
options: Removing the cap proteins entirely
Doubling the number of wall repeat units
A single point mutation near the cap that blocked closure, producing open, rosette-shaped particles
Switching the expression host from E. coli to yeast
questions.explanation: A single mutation near the cap prevented the three-tiered closure, leaving open rosette shapes instead of sealed shells — direct evidence that this region is responsible for sealing the vault.

posts.title: Inside Anthropic's Defenses Against Distillation Attacks
posts.subtitle: How a reasoning lockdown, a classifier, and mass account bans cut stolen reasoning 10x-100x.
posts.summary: Anthropic published a detailed account of how it's fighting distillation attacks — large-scale, fraudulent-account campaigns that extract a frontier model's reasoning to clone its capabilities into cheaper, less-safeguarded models. Three layered defenses (reasoning lockdown, an extraction classifier, and aggressive account bans) cut extracted reasoning tokens by 10x to 100x or more, though Anthropic frames it as an ongoing cat-and-mouse fight, not a solved problem.

slides.title: Someone Is Quietly Cloning Frontier Models at Scale
slides.body: Distillation attacks extract a frontier model's capabilities through networks of fraudulent accounts, then bake them into a cheaper competitor model. Anthropic just published how it's fighting back — with real numbers behind the fight.

slides.title: Why Distillation Is a Safety Problem, Not Just a Business One
bullets: Distillation lets a developer copy a frontier model's capabilities at a fraction of the training cost, often through networks of fraudulent accounts.
Distilled models can ship without the original's safety guardrails — concentrating risk in domains like bioweapons and cyber capability.
Anthropic says distilled capabilities have shown up in foreign military, intelligence, and surveillance systems.
Scale of the abuse: one proxy network ran over 20,000 fraudulent accounts at once; another sent 12,000 requests designed to extract Claude's reasoning.

slides.title: Two Named Examples From the Report
bullets: Zhipu (GLM-5.3): allegedly distilled cyber capabilities from US models; after Anthropic's safeguards degraded its attacks on Claude Fable 5, it switched to an older Claude model and another lab's model instead.
CAISI later assessed GLM-5.3 as the most cyber-capable open-weights model released to date.

Moonshot's Kimi: some user requests were secretly forwarded to Claude — one reportedly from a user Anthropic believes was linked to China's PLA, seeking to analyze CCTV surveillance of a specific individual.

slides.title: Defense 1: Lock Down Where Reasoning Can Travel
bullets: Earlier approach — showing users a summary instead of full reasoning — cost real capability: a model trained on full transcripts hit 80.4% on SWE-bench Verified versus 71.8% trained on summaries.
So attackers shifted to pressuring Claude directly to reveal full reasoning verbatim through proxy accounts.

New fix, 'preserved thinking' (shipped with Claude Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5): blocks new API accounts created on or after August 31, 2026 from editing Claude's prior context, breaking the repeated-extraction loop.
With Sonnet 5.5, raw reasoning transcripts are visible only to the organization whose request produced them.

slides.title: Defense 2 & 3: Catch the Attempt, Then Make It Expensive
bullets: A two-stage classifier, built on Anthropic's constitutional-classifiers research, detects reasoning-extraction attempts with a false-positive rate under 0.1%, and robustness the company compares to its bioweapons safeguard tier.
It adapts quickly to new evasion tricks — e.g. asking Claude to translate its reasoning into another language or wrap it in disguised tags.
Repeat offenders face stricter limits or bans; tens of thousands of distillation-linked accounts have been removed, often within 2 hours of a campaign starting.
Since September 24, 2026, Anthropic charges for requests its safeguards block before Claude even responds — turning extraction attempts into a cost, not a free trial.

slides.title: The Measured Effect

rows: 10x-100x+ lower; some days too small to measure
tens of thousands, often within 2 hours

slides.title: This Isn't a Solved Problem
bullets: Real cost: some benign developers get blocked or must update integrations, and under 0.1% of legitimate requests are still misclassified.
Anthropic frames this as an ongoing 'cat-and-mouse game' — it has not seen a highly sophisticated, persistent bypass yet, but doesn't claim a final defense.
Industry incentive problem: distillers are often paying customers, so other platforms have weak incentive to police them. Publishing the method is partly meant to pressure the industry to follow.

slides.title: Why This Matters Beyond Anthropic
bullets: This is a detailed, numbers-backed playbook for stopping model extraction at scale — not just a policy statement.
It ties model safety directly to national-security framing: distilled capability reaching foreign cyber or surveillance systems is a new kind of release risk.
If you build on any frontier API, expect reasoning visibility and account-level scrutiny to keep tightening across the industry.

questions.prompt: What happened when Anthropic trained a model on summarized reasoning instead of full transcripts?
options: Performance improved to 85% on SWE-bench Verified
Performance dropped to 71.8% on SWE-bench Verified, down from 80.4% with full transcripts
There was no measurable difference in performance
The model became fully immune to distillation
questions.explanation: Summarizing reasoning cost real capability (80.4% to 71.8% on SWE-bench Verified), which is why Anthropic couldn't simply hide reasoning by default and had to build more targeted defenses instead.

questions.prompt: What does Anthropic's 'preserved thinking' defense specifically block?
options: All API access to reasoning tokens for every account, everywhere
New API accounts (created on or after August 31, 2026) from editing Claude's prior context, which prevents repeated extraction
Any use of Claude outside the United States
Third-party fine-tuning of any Claude model
questions.explanation: Preserved thinking targets the exact mechanism distillers relied on — repeatedly editing and replaying context to pressure out full reasoning — rather than blocking reasoning access outright.

questions.prompt: How effective was the two-stage extraction classifier, according to the reported numbers?
options: It eliminated distillation completely with zero false positives
Extracted reasoning tokens fell 10x to 100x or more, with a false-positive rate under 0.1%
It only worked against Claude Opus, not other Claude models
It increased extraction attempts by making reasoning easier to access
questions.explanation: The classifier drove a 10x-to-100x-plus drop in extracted reasoning tokens while keeping false positives under 0.1% — a large effect with a tightly bounded cost to legitimate users.

posts.title: Consistent Hashing: Scaling Without a Full Reshuffle
posts.subtitle: The hash-ring trick that keeps most of your cache keys in place when a node joins or leaves.
posts.summary: Naive hash-based sharding (hash(key) % N) remaps almost every key whenever the number of servers changes, causing a cache-wide stampede. Consistent hashing places both servers and keys on a shared hash ring so a resize only moves the keys near the changed node — roughly 1/N of them — and virtual nodes keep that load evenly spread across real hardware.

slides.title: One Idea Fixes Distributed Caching's Worst Day
slides.body: Add or remove one server from a naive hash-based cache cluster, and almost every key moves to a new machine — a cache-wide stampede. Consistent hashing was designed specifically to stop that.

slides.title: Modulo Hashing Breaks Almost Everything on Resize
bullets: Naive sharding: server = hash(key) % N. Simple and fast — until N changes.
Going from 4 servers to 5 remaps roughly 4 out of every 5 keys to a different machine, even though only one server was added.
Every remapped key is a guaranteed cache miss: a stampede of requests hits the origin database all at once.
This is the exact problem Karger et al. set out to solve in 1997 for web caching — the technique that underpins Akamai's CDN.

slides.title: Put Servers and Keys on the Same Ring
bullets: Hash both servers and keys into the same fixed output space (e.g. 0 to 2^32-1) and arrange that space as a circle.
A key belongs to the first server whose position on the ring is reached by walking clockwise from the key's own hash.
Add a server: it only intercepts keys between itself and the previous node going counter-clockwise — nothing else moves.
Remove a server: only its keys fall through to the next node on the ring; every other server's keys are untouched.

slides.title: Virtual Nodes Fix the Uneven-Ring Problem
bullets: With just 1 hash position per physical server, ring segments are wildly uneven by pure chance — one server can end up with 2x another's load.
Fix: hash each physical server into many points on the ring (100-200 'virtual nodes' is typical — this is what Amazon's Dynamo paper and Cassandra both do).
More virtual nodes smooths load distribution, at the cost of more routing metadata to store and look up.
This also handles unequal hardware: give a bigger server more virtual nodes instead of special-casing it in code.

slides.title: Worked Example: Adding a 4th Cache Node
slides.body: Ring positions (0-99) for 3 servers: A=10, B=40, C=75. Four keys hash to 5, 35, 48, and 95.
bullets: Adding server D at position 55 only steals keys in the arc between B (40) and D (55) that used to belong to C — here, just k3.
3 of 4 keys never move. A modulo-hash resize from 3 to 4 servers would have remapped about 3 of those 4 keys instead.

slides.title: Consistent Hashing vs. the Alternatives

rows: Simple sharded setups, rarely at production scale
Some load balancers and CDN request routers

slides.title: When It's Not the Right Tool
bullets: Doesn't fix hot keys — if one key draws 1000x the traffic of others, moving it to a different node doesn't spread that load out.
Routing requires every client (or a coordinator) to agree on the current ring layout, which adds operational complexity versus a single static lookup table.
For small, rarely-resized clusters — say, 3 fixed database shards — a static lookup table is simpler, and consistent hashing is overkill.
Replication needs its own policy on top of the ring: consistent hashing decides where a key's primary copy lives, not how many replicas to keep.

slides.title: The Core Idea, Compressed
bullets: Map servers and keys into the same hash space; a key belongs to the nearest server found by walking clockwise on the ring.
Resizing moves roughly 1/N of keys instead of nearly all of them — that's the entire point.
Use virtual nodes (100-200 per server) in any real deployment, or load distribution gets lumpy.
It's the backbone of Dynamo, Cassandra, and most CDNs — understanding it explains how they add capacity without a cache-wide stampede.

questions.prompt: In consistent hashing, which server does a given key belong to?
options: The server with the numerically closest hash value in either direction
The first server whose position on the ring is reached by walking clockwise from the key's hash position
A randomly chosen server, re-rolled on every request
Whichever server currently has the lowest load
questions.explanation: Ownership is directional — walk clockwise from the key's hash position until you hit a server. That directionality is exactly what limits the blast radius when a server is added or removed to one contiguous arc of the ring.

questions.prompt: Why do real systems like Cassandra and DynamoDB give each physical server 100-200 'virtual nodes' instead of one ring position?
options: To make the ring harder for attackers to map
A single position per server leaves ring segments uneven by chance; many virtual nodes average that out into smoother load
Virtual nodes are required for the hash function to work at all
To automatically determine how many replicas to keep
questions.explanation: With one position per server, pure chance can hand one server a huge arc and another a tiny one. Spreading each physical server across 100-200 ring positions averages that imbalance out.

questions.prompt: A cluster grows from 4 servers to 5. Roughly what fraction of keys gets remapped under consistent hashing versus naive modulo hashing (hash % N)?
options: About 1/5 under consistent hashing versus roughly 4/5 under modulo hashing
Both approaches remap close to 100% of keys
Consistent hashing remaps more keys than modulo hashing
Neither approach remaps any keys when a server is added
questions.explanation: Consistent hashing only moves the keys in the arc now owned by the new node, roughly 1/N of them. Modulo hashing's mapping has no such locality, so adding one server to five scrambles the assignment for most keys.

posts.title: Decoding Strategies: How LLMs Pick the Next Token
posts.subtitle: Greedy decoding is deterministic and boring — temperature, top-k, and top-p reshape or truncate the probability distribution to control how much the model gambles on its next word.
posts.summary: Every LLM call ends with a choice: which token comes next. Greedy decoding always picks the single most likely token, producing repetitive, deterministic text. Temperature, top-k, and top-p reshape or truncate the probability distribution before sampling, trading determinism for diversity — and picking the wrong setting can make a model either loop forever or hallucinate nonsense.

slides.title: A Language Model's Last Step Is a Dice Roll
slides.body: After the final layer, an LLM outputs a probability for every token in its vocabulary. What happens next — argmax, or something more interesting — is called decoding, and it shapes everything about the output's style and reliability.
bullets: The model itself never 'decides' a word — a separate sampling procedure converts its raw probabilities into a chosen token
The exact same model weights can sound robotic or wildly creative, depending only on the decoding settings
Three knobs — temperature, top-k, top-p — are the ones nearly every API exposes

slides.title: Greedy Decoding Gets Stuck in Loops
slides.body: The simplest strategy — always pick the highest-probability token (argmax) — sounds safe, but it has a well-known failure mode.
bullets: Greedy decoding is fully deterministic: same prompt, same output, every time
It tends to produce repetitive, bland text — once a phrase becomes locally 'most likely,' the model keeps re-choosing it, looping in extreme cases
It can't express genuine uncertainty: if two tokens are 51% and 49% likely, greedy throws away the 49% option entirely, every single time

slides.title: Temperature Rescales the Distribution Before Sampling
slides.body: Temperature (T) divides each token's logit before the softmax turns logits into probabilities: p_i = exp(logit_i / T) / Σ exp(logit_j / T).
bullets: T < 1 sharpens the distribution — the gap between likely and unlikely tokens grows, pushing sampling toward argmax (T→0 becomes greedy decoding)
T > 1 flattens the distribution — low-probability tokens get a real chance, increasing diversity but also incoherence
T = 1 leaves the model's raw distribution untouched
Temperature never removes any token from consideration — it only reshapes probabilities across the full vocabulary

slides.title: Top-k and Top-p Cut the Candidate Pool First
slides.body: Where temperature reshapes the whole distribution, top-k and top-p throw away the long tail before sampling even happens.
bullets: Top-k keeps only the k highest-probability tokens, renormalizes just those, and samples from that fixed-size pool (common default: k = 40-50)
Top-p (nucleus sampling) instead keeps the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability reaches p — e.g. p = 0.9 — and the pool size changes every step
Top-p adapts automatically: when the model is very confident (one token near 99%), the nucleus is tiny; when it's uncertain (a flat distribution), the nucleus widens to include many tokens
Top-k's fixed pool size is its weakness: k = 50 is huge when the model is confident, and too small when it's genuinely torn between hundreds of plausible tokens

slides.title: Four Strategies, Side by Side
slides.body: Most production APIs combine temperature with top-p (and sometimes top-k) rather than relying on just one knob.

slides.title: Walking Through One Token Choice
slides.body: Suppose the model's next-token distribution is: 'cat' 0.50, 'dog' 0.30, 'fish' 0.10, 'rock' 0.06, 'cloud' 0.04.
bullets: Greedy: always picks 'cat' — no exceptions, ever
Top-k=2: pool is {'cat','dog'} (0.50+0.30=0.80), renormalized to roughly 'cat' 0.625 / 'dog' 0.375 — 'fish', 'rock', 'cloud' can never be chosen
Top-p=0.9: keeps adding tokens until cumulative probability passes 0.9 — that's 'cat'+'dog'+'fish'+'rock' (0.50+0.30+0.10+0.06=0.96 ≥ 0.9), so only 'cloud' is excluded
Temperature=1.5 applied before either cutoff flattens the gaps, so 'fish', 'rock', even 'cloud' become meaningfully more likely to survive and get sampled

slides.title: Picking the Wrong Setting Breaks Different Things
slides.body: There's no single 'correct' setting — the right choice depends entirely on the task.
bullets: Too low (near-greedy): safe for code generation and structured output where syntax must be exact, but prone to repetition loops in long-form text
Too high (T > 1.3, or top-p near 1.0 with a wide k): creative writing benefits from the diversity, but code and factual answers start hallucinating invalid syntax or invented facts
Stacking settings carelessly compounds the effect — high temperature AND high top-p AND high top-k together removes almost every safety net on the output
Most coding assistants default to T ≈ 0-0.3; most chat assistants default to T ≈ 0.7-1.0 with top-p ≈ 0.9 as the standard starting point

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Decoding is a separate step from the model itself — the same weights can sound deterministic or wildly creative depending only on these settings
Temperature reshapes probabilities across the whole vocabulary; top-k and top-p instead cut the tail before sampling even starts
Top-p adapts its candidate pool size to the model's confidence at each step; top-k's pool size stays fixed regardless of confidence
Low settings favor correctness-critical tasks (code, facts); higher settings favor creative, open-ended tasks — and stacking extremes compounds both the benefits and the risks

questions.prompt: What does setting temperature very close to 0 do to next-token sampling?
options: It makes the output more random and diverse
It sharply amplifies logit differences, making sampling nearly indistinguishable from greedy (argmax) decoding
It increases the model's effective vocabulary size
It disables the softmax step entirely
questions.explanation: Dividing logits by a very small T exaggerates the gaps between them, so after softmax the distribution collapses toward a one-hot vector on the highest-probability token — functionally the same as greedy decoding.

questions.prompt: How does top-p (nucleus) sampling differ from top-k sampling?
options: Top-p always samples from exactly p tokens, same as top-k's fixed k
Top-p dynamically sizes the candidate pool to the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability reaches p, while top-k uses a fixed pool size
Top-p ignores the model's probability distribution entirely
Top-p can only be used with greedy decoding
questions.explanation: Top-k always keeps exactly k tokens no matter how confident the model is, while top-p grows or shrinks its candidate set every step based on how the probability mass is actually distributed — a tiny nucleus when the model is sure, a wide one when it's torn.

questions.prompt: Why do most coding assistants default to a low temperature (around 0-0.3) rather than a high one?
options: Low temperature makes inference run faster on the GPU
Low temperature reduces the API's token cost
Code has rigid syntax, so sampling low-probability tokens more often breaks compilation or introduces hallucinated APIs
High temperature disables top-p sampling
questions.explanation: Unlike prose, code fails hard on small mistakes — a single wrong token can break syntax or call a function that doesn't exist — so coding tools bias heavily toward the model's highest-confidence tokens rather than exploring the tail of the distribution.

posts.title: SpecPilot: An Agent That Tunes Its Own Speculative Decoding
posts.subtitle: An agentic search loop pushed one speculative-decoding stack from 4.46x to 10.87x over plain autoregressive decoding — without changing a single output token.
posts.summary: SpecPilot is an agentic loop that automatically finds lossless speedups in already-deployed speculative decoding systems, raising one setup's speedup over autoregressive decoding from 4.46x to 10.87x. It works by repeatedly finding the biggest gap to a theoretical speed ceiling, dispatching agents to close it, and verifying every change keeps outputs identical to the stock model before keeping it.

slides.title: Speculative Decoding Still Leaves Speed on the Table
slides.body: Teams ship a speculative decoder once and move on. SpecPilot treats that shipped system as a starting point, not a finish line, and keeps optimizing it automatically.
bullets: On an RTX PRO 6000, the shipped speculative decoder hit 4.46x over autoregressive decoding
SpecPilot's agentic search pushed the same deployment to 10.87x — 2.44x faster than the stock system
Every optimization is verified lossless: outputs must match the target model exactly

slides.title: Why Shipped Speculative Decoders Underperform
slides.body: Speculative decoding already speeds up generation by having a cheap draft model propose tokens that a bigger target model verifies in parallel. But the released configuration is usually a fixed, generic setup.
bullets: Draft-model settings (tree shape, draft length) are tuned once for a generic workload, not the specific GPU and batch size in production
GPU kernels often run far from the hardware's memory-bandwidth roofline, wasting cycles the draft/verify loop could use
No one keeps re-tuning after launch, so the gap between 'what's deployed' and 'what's physically possible' just sits there unclaimed

slides.title: An Agentic Loop That Hunts the Gap to the Ceiling
slides.body: Each round, SpecPilot computes a cost model of the current system versus its theoretical ceiling, then dispatches agents at exactly the biggest gap.
bullets: A cost model identifies where the deployment is furthest from its roofline each round — kernel latency, draft acceptance rate, batching overhead
Parallel agents propose fixes; a dedicated kernel sub-agent retunes GPU kernels that are far from their memory-bandwidth limit
A structured memory carries validated mechanisms forward across rounds and across different model/hardware deployments, so later searches reuse earlier discoveries

slides.title: Token Forcing: How It Stays Lossless While Changing Everything
slides.body: Speed means nothing if the model starts saying different things. SpecPilot's safety net is 'token forcing.'
bullets: Every candidate optimization is checked by forcing its output tokens against what the stock target model would have produced
If outputs diverge, the change is rejected — only mechanisms that are provably lossless get kept in memory
This is why SpecPilot can mutate kernels, draft trees, and batching strategy aggressively: the verification step is the real speed limit, not caution

slides.title: The Numbers: Stock vs. SpecPilot-Tuned, Single Request
slides.body: Speedups are measured over plain autoregressive (AR) decoding, 2048 new tokens, single concurrent request.
bullets: Gains hold across two different draft systems (DFlash2, DSpark) and two different GPUs
The smallest gain over stock (2.24x) was still on the fastest stock baseline (H100)

slides.title: Same Optimization, Different Hardware, Different Fix
slides.body: On the RTX PRO 6000, Qwen3.8-27B with DFlash2 starts at 4.46x over AR — a weaker stock baseline than on H100, because the consumer GPU's memory bandwidth bottlenecks the draft/verify loop differently.
bullets: SpecPilot's cost model flags the RTX PRO 6000 run as furthest from its kernel roofline, so the kernel sub-agent is dispatched first here
After retuning, this deployment reaches the highest absolute speedup in the whole study: 10.87x over AR

The structured memory from this run — 'this kernel pattern helps on memory-bandwidth-limited consumer GPUs' — carries over to the Muse-Glimmer-30B run on the same hardware, which lands at a similar 10.63x

slides.title: Where the Gains Shrink
slides.body: SpecPilot's biggest wins are on single-request, latency-focused serving. Batched, throughput-focused serving tells a different story.
bullets: Under batching (16-24 concurrent requests, H100, FP8), stock already reaches ~2x over AR — SpecPilot adds roughly another 2x on top, smaller relative gains than single-request mode

The paper's own accuracy sanity check (24-question set) shows AR scoring highest (177-178/240 in batching), stock close behind, SpecPilot slightly lower (167-172/240) — a reminder that 'lossless vs. the stock speculative decoder' isn't the same as 'identical to AR,' since no speculative decoder (stock included) is bitwise identical to AR
Running the agentic search itself costs real compute — it's worth paying for a high-traffic deployment, not a one-off experiment

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: SpecPilot treats a shipped speculative-decoding system as a starting point, finding and closing the gap to its theoretical speed ceiling automatically
Token forcing — checking every change against the stock target model's outputs — is what lets it optimize aggressively while staying lossless
Measured gains: 2.24x-2.52x faster than already-shipped speculative decoders, reaching up to 10.87x over plain autoregressive decoding
Gains are largest for single-request, latency-sensitive serving; batched, throughput-focused serving sees smaller relative improvement

questions.prompt: What does SpecPilot's cost model decide each round?
options: Which users get priority access to the GPU
Where the current deployment is furthest from its theoretical speed ceiling, so agents can target that gap
How many tokens the draft model should generate per user request
Whether to switch to a completely different base model
questions.explanation: SpecPilot's loop is driven by a cost model that measures the gap between the current system and its roofline each round, then dispatches agents (including a kernel sub-agent) at exactly that gap — not a fixed checklist of fixes.

questions.prompt: How does SpecPilot guarantee its optimizations don't change what the model outputs?
options: It never changes anything about the draft model
It uses token forcing — checking candidate changes' outputs against the stock target model, and rejecting any that diverge
It runs every optimization through a second, independent LLM for approval
It limits itself to optimizations that have been published in a peer-reviewed paper
questions.explanation: Token forcing is the verification mechanism: any optimization that doesn't reproduce the stock target model's outputs exactly is discarded, which is what lets SpecPilot aggressively retune kernels and draft strategy without risking correctness.

questions.prompt: Based on the results table, which statement is accurate?
options: SpecPilot's gains over stock speculative decoding were roughly 2.2x-2.5x across the tested single-request deployments
SpecPilot only helped on one of the four tested deployments
SpecPilot's speedups were identical regardless of GPU or draft system used
Stock speculative decoding already matched SpecPilot's performance on H100
questions.explanation: Across H100 and RTX PRO 6000, with both DFlash2 and DSpark drafters, SpecPilot's gain over the already-shipped (stock) speculative decoder landed between roughly 2.24x and 2.52x in single-request mode.

posts.title: Speculative Decoding: Guessing Ahead to Skip the Wait
posts.subtitle: A cheap draft model proposes several tokens at once; the big model checks them all in a single forward pass — and the math guarantees you get exactly the same output either way.
posts.summary: Autoregressive decoding generates one token per full forward pass through the model, which wastes most of a GPU's compute waiting on memory. Speculative decoding lets a small draft model guess several tokens ahead, then verifies them against the big model in one parallel pass, accepting whatever prefix matches and resampling the rest — with no change to the final output distribution.

slides.title: One Token Per Forward Pass Is the Real Bottleneck
slides.body: Every token an LLM generates normally costs one full pass through every layer of the model. Speculative decoding breaks that one-token-per-pass rule without changing what the model says.
bullets: A full forward pass to produce a single token leaves most GPU compute idle, waiting on memory bandwidth
Speculative decoding can produce several tokens per big-model pass instead of one
The output distribution is mathematically identical to normal decoding — this is not an approximation

slides.title: Why Autoregressive Generation Is Memory-Bound, Not Compute-Bound
slides.body: People assume LLM inference is slow because the model is 'doing a lot of math.' During token-by-token generation, the real limiter is different.
bullets: Generating one token needs the model's full weights streamed from GPU memory, but only a tiny batch (often size 1) to multiply against them
The GPU's compute units sit mostly idle during that pass — the bottleneck is how fast weights can be read from memory, not how fast the matrix multiplies run
Because this happens once per output token, generation latency scales linearly with output length, serially, with no way to parallelize across tokens the normal way

slides.title: Draft, Then Verify in Parallel
slides.body: Speculative decoding splits generation into two roles: a small, fast draft model that guesses ahead, and the original big model that checks the guesses.
bullets: The draft model autoregressively proposes k tokens (cheap, since it's small)
The target model runs ONE forward pass over all k draft tokens plus the real context — the same memory-bound pass now checks k+1 positions at once instead of 1

Rejection sampling compares each draft token's probability under the target model; accept the longest correct prefix, then resample a replacement for the first mismatch from the target's own distribution
This resampling step is exactly why the output distribution matches standard decoding exactly — it's a mathematical guarantee, not a heuristic

slides.title: Walking Through One Verification Step
slides.body: Say the draft model proposes 5 tokens for "The capital of France is Par-is , which". The target model checks all 5 in one pass.
bullets: Target model agrees with draft tokens 1-3 ("is", "Par", "is") — those are accepted for free, no extra forward pass needed
At token 4, the draft guessed "," but the target model's distribution favors a different token — the draft is rejected here
The target resamples token 4 from its own distribution (adjusted for what was rejected), and the draft model restarts guessing from there
Net result: 3 tokens produced for the cost of 1 target forward pass instead of 3 — the speedup scales with how often the draft guesses right

slides.title: The Draft-Model Design Space
slides.body: Different techniques change how the draft tokens are produced, trading complexity for acceptance rate.
bullets: A separate, smaller model in the same family tends to have higher token-agreement with the target than an unrelated small model
Tree-based methods (speculating multiple candidate continuations, not just one chain) raise the accepted-tokens-per-pass count further, at the cost of a bigger verification pass

rows: Simple, needs two models loaded and kept in sync
Earlier layers of the same model
No second model, but lower acceptance rate than a dedicated draft model
Higher accepted-tokens-per-pass, costs a wider verification pass

slides.title: When the Speedup Shrinks
slides.body: Speculative decoding's win depends entirely on how often the draft model guesses what the target would have said.
bullets: Highly predictable text (boilerplate code, repeated structure, common phrases) gets accepted often — big speedups
Open-ended, creative, or unusual text gets rejected more often, shrinking the benefit toward zero

At large batch sizes, the target model's forward pass becomes compute-bound instead of memory-bound, so the 'free parallel verification' advantage shrinks — the biggest wins are in low-batch, latency-sensitive serving
You now have two models to keep loaded and aligned, plus a verification step to implement correctly — it's not free engineering complexity

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: LLM token generation is memory-bandwidth-bound, not compute-bound — most GPU compute sits idle per token
Speculative decoding has a cheap draft model guess ahead, then verifies all guesses in one parallel pass through the big model
Rejection sampling guarantees the final output distribution is mathematically identical to plain decoding — no quality tradeoff
The speedup depends on draft-acceptance rate: high for predictable text and low batch sizes, shrinking for creative text and large batches

questions.prompt: Why is single-token autoregressive generation usually memory-bandwidth-bound rather than compute-bound?
options: GPUs cannot perform matrix multiplication fast enough for language models
Each step streams the full model weights from memory to multiply against a tiny batch, leaving compute units mostly idle
The model's vocabulary is too large to fit in memory
Token generation requires recomputing gradients at every step
questions.explanation: Decoding one token needs the entire set of weights read from GPU memory, but only a small amount of actual computation (often batch size 1), so the GPU spends most of its time waiting on memory bandwidth rather than doing math.

questions.prompt: Why does speculative decoding produce exactly the same output distribution as standard decoding?
options: Because the draft model is a smaller, less accurate copy that averages out errors
Because rejection sampling only accepts a draft token if it matches the target distribution, and resamples mismatches directly from the target model's own distribution
Because the target model is run twice to double-check every token
It doesn't — speculative decoding trades a small amount of accuracy for speed
questions.explanation: The accept/reject/resample procedure is a form of rejection sampling: accepted tokens are confirmed matches, and any rejected token is replaced by one sampled from the target model's own distribution — a mathematical guarantee that the overall output distribution is unchanged.

questions.prompt: Which scenario benefits LEAST from speculative decoding?
options: A coding assistant autocompleting a common boilerplate pattern
A low-batch-size, single-user chat session
A high-batch-size serving setup generating highly creative, unpredictable text
A customer-support bot responding with frequently repeated phrasing
questions.explanation: At large batch sizes, the target model's verification pass becomes compute-bound instead of memory-bound, erasing the 'free parallel check' advantage, and creative/unpredictable text has a low draft-acceptance rate — both effects shrink the speedup toward zero.

posts.title: Knowledge Distillation: Training Small Models to Mimic Big Ones
posts.subtitle: A 66M-parameter student can keep ~97% of a 110M teacher's accuracy by learning from its softened probabilities, not just its right answers.
posts.summary: Knowledge distillation trains a small 'student' model to reproduce a large 'teacher' model's full output distribution, not just its hard labels — transferring the teacher's uncertainty and inter-class relationships ('dark knowledge') into a fraction of the parameters. Done well, the student keeps most of the teacher's accuracy at a fraction of its size and latency; done poorly, it plateaus far below what distillation promised.

slides.title: Why Train a Model to Copy Another Model?
slides.body: The best-performing model you have is often too big, slow, or expensive to actually deploy. Distillation keeps most of its intelligence in a model small enough to ship.

slides.title: Big Models Win Benchmarks, Then Lose in Production
slides.body: A 70B model might top every leaderboard, but it doesn't fit on a phone, costs too much per request, and adds latency users notice.
bullets: Serving cost and latency scale roughly with parameter count — a 10x bigger model is roughly 10x more GPU-seconds per token
Mobile and edge deployments have hard memory ceilings that quantization alone can't fix
Training a small model from scratch on the same labeled data rarely matches a distilled model's accuracy

slides.title: The Student Learns the Teacher's Uncertainty, Not Just Its Answer
slides.body: A hard label says 'this is a cat.' The teacher's full output distribution says '95% cat, 4% dog, 1% fox' — that small residual encodes real information about what the model finds similar.
bullets: The teacher's logits are divided by a temperature T > 1 before softmax, softening the distribution so small probabilities survive instead of rounding to ~0
The student trains on a weighted sum of two losses: KL-divergence to the softened teacher distribution, plus ordinary cross-entropy against the true label
Hinton et al. called this extra signal 'dark knowledge' — it's why distilled students often beat students trained from scratch on the same labels

slides.title: Real Numbers: How Much Does Distillation Actually Cost You?
slides.body: Two well-known BERT distillations show the tradeoff curve: how much size and speed you buy, and how much accuracy you give up for it.
bullets: DistilBERT halves the layer count (12 → 6) and initializes the student from every other teacher layer
TinyBERT pushes much further by also matching intermediate hidden states and attention maps, not just final logits

slides.title: Shipping a Model That Actually Fits on the Device
slides.body: A voice-assistant team needs on-device intent classification but can't ship a multi-billion-parameter LLM to a phone.
bullets: They run millions of unlabeled, real user utterances through the large teacher model to generate soft-label probability distributions
A 350M-parameter student is trained on those soft labels plus a small set of human-verified hard labels
The shipped student hits sub-50ms on-device latency while keeping the vast majority of the teacher's intent accuracy — something a student trained only on the small hard-labeled set couldn't match

slides.title: The Distillation Ceiling — and When Not to Bother
slides.body: Distillation transfers knowledge; it doesn't create it. The student is bounded by what the teacher actually knows, and by how much capacity gap the training process can bridge.
bullets: A student almost never exceeds its teacher's accuracy — and if the capacity gap is extreme (e.g. 1000x fewer parameters), accuracy can collapse instead of gracefully degrading
Classic logit-based distillation needs access to the teacher's probability distribution, not just its generated text — impossible against a closed API that only returns final output
The student inherits the teacher's biases and blind spots exactly, since it's trained to match them
Skip it when you already have abundant labeled data and compute to train the small model directly — plain supervised training is simpler and avoids transferring teacher bias

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Distillation trains a small student to match a large teacher's full output distribution, not just its final label
Temperature-softened softmax reveals 'dark knowledge' — relative similarity between wrong classes — that hard labels throw away
Real systems (DistilBERT, TinyBERT) show you can cut params 40-90% while keeping ~97% of accuracy
It needs the teacher's logits, has a ceiling at the teacher's own accuracy, and inherits the teacher's biases

questions.prompt: What is 'dark knowledge' in knowledge distillation?
options: The teacher's training data, hidden from the student
The relative probabilities the teacher assigns to wrong classes, revealing which classes it finds similar
A regularization trick unrelated to the teacher model
The student's own uncertainty before any training happens
questions.explanation: A one-hot label discards everything except the right answer. The teacher's softened distribution keeps the relative weight it puts on wrong classes — e.g. 'dog' getting more probability than 'car' when the true label is 'cat' — and that structure is what the student learns to copy.

questions.prompt: Why does distillation divide the teacher's logits by a temperature T > 1 before applying softmax?
options: To make the output distribution sharper and more confident
To speed up the student's training loop
To soften the distribution so smaller, informative probabilities don't round to near-zero
To convert the logits directly into token IDs
questions.explanation: Raw softmax on a confident teacher puts almost all probability mass on the top class, hiding the 'dark knowledge' in the rest. Dividing by T > 1 flattens the distribution so the smaller probabilities carry a learnable signal.

questions.prompt: Which scenario makes classic logit-based distillation impossible?
options: The teacher and student use different architectures
The teacher is only reachable through a closed API that returns generated text, not logits
The student has fewer parameters than the teacher
The training dataset has no human labels at all
questions.explanation: Logit-based distillation needs the teacher's probability distribution over classes or tokens. A black-box API that only returns final text gives you no distribution to match — you'd need an alternative like training on the generated text itself, which is a different, weaker technique.

posts.title: Hybrid Search: Why Vector Search Alone Misses Exact Matches
posts.subtitle: Dense embeddings find meaning; sparse keyword search finds exact codes and names — fusing both beats either alone.
posts.summary: Dense vector search is built for semantic similarity and is weak on exact tokens — error codes, SKUs, names — exactly where keyword search (BM25) excels. Hybrid search runs both retrievers in parallel and fuses their ranked lists, typically with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, to get the strengths of each without retraining either one.

slides.title: Your Vector Search Just Missed the One Exact Match That Mattered
slides.body: A user searches for error code 'E04-220'. The dense retriever returns five semantically similar troubleshooting docs — none of which mention E04-220.

slides.title: Embeddings Generalize — Sometimes Too Much
slides.body: Dense vector search is built to find semantic similarity, which means it can blur exactly the tokens that matter most: IDs, codes, acronyms, and rare proper nouns.
bullets: A dense embedding for 'E04-220' sits close to other error-code-shaped strings — the model has no reason to treat this exact code as special
Short, rare, or out-of-vocabulary terms (SKUs, product codes, names) are exactly where embedding models have the least training signal
Pure semantic search can rank a fluent, topically-similar wrong document above the one document with the literal match

slides.title: Run a Keyword Retriever and a Vector Retriever in Parallel
slides.body: Hybrid search pairs a sparse lexical retriever (BM25) with a dense vector retriever, then merges their two ranked lists instead of picking one.
bullets: BM25 scores a document higher the more it contains the query's exact terms, weighted down for terms common across almost every document (inverse document frequency)
The dense retriever scores by similarity between query and document embeddings — strong on paraphrase and meaning, weak on exact tokens
Each retriever returns its own top-k ranked list; neither has to 'win' outright before fusion

slides.title: Fusing Two Ranked Lists Without Retraining Either One
slides.body: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) is the standard way to merge BM25 and vector rankings: score each document by summing 1/(k + rank) across both lists, using a constant k (commonly 60) to dampen any single list's influence.
bullets: RRF needs no score normalization — it only looks at rank position, so BM25 scores and cosine similarities (different, incomparable scales) never need to be reconciled directly
A document ranked reasonably well in BOTH lists usually outscores one ranked #1 in only one of them

rows: Extra infra: two indexes, one fusion step

slides.title: Error-Code Search: Hybrid Gets It Right Where Dense Alone Fails
slides.body: A support team indexes 50,000 troubleshooting articles with both a BM25 index and a dense vector index.
bullets: Query: 'E04-220 won't clear after reset' — BM25 ranks the one article containing the exact code at #1, because that token is rare across the corpus (high IDF)
The dense retriever ranks that same article #14, behind more generic 'won't clear after reset' articles with no code match
RRF fusion: the article at rank 1 (BM25) and rank 14 (dense) still outscores an article ranked #2 by dense but absent from BM25's list — because it's strong in one list and present in both

slides.title: Hybrid Search Isn't Free — Know When to Skip It
slides.body: Running two retrievers means two indexes to build, store, and keep in sync, plus a fusion step to tune.
bullets: It doubles indexing infrastructure and adds the latency of querying both systems before fusing results
The fusion constant k and any per-retriever weighting need tuning on real queries — defaults don't transfer blindly across domains
If a corpus has almost no exact-match-sensitive queries (pure prose, no codes/IDs/names, all-paraphrase search), plain dense retrieval may be simpler with little accuracy loss
Hybrid fuses two retrievers — it doesn't fix a bad chunking strategy or a genuinely out-of-domain query

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: BM25 and dense retrieval fail on opposite query types: exact tokens vs. paraphrased meaning
Hybrid search runs both and fuses the ranked lists, most commonly with Reciprocal Rank Fusion
RRF compares rank positions, not raw scores, so it sidesteps the BM25-vs-cosine scale mismatch
The extra infrastructure only pays off when real queries actually mix exact-match and semantic intent

questions.prompt: Why do BM25 and dense vector retrievers tend to fail on different kinds of queries?
options: BM25 is just an older, strictly worse version of dense retrieval
BM25 rewards exact term overlap and rare-term specificity, while dense retrieval rewards semantic similarity and can blur exact, rare tokens
Dense retrieval cannot be used for text at all, only images
BM25 requires a GPU and dense retrieval does not
questions.explanation: BM25's scoring is built directly from term frequency and inverse document frequency, so rare exact terms (codes, IDs) score highly. Dense embeddings are trained to capture meaning, which is exactly what makes them weak at distinguishing one rare exact token from a similarly-shaped one.

questions.prompt: What does Reciprocal Rank Fusion actually combine from the two retrievers?
options: The raw cosine similarity and BM25 scores, averaged directly
Each document's rank position in each list, summed as 1/(k + rank)
A machine-learned re-ranking model trained on click data
Only the top-1 result from whichever retriever runs faster
questions.explanation: RRF deliberately avoids combining raw scores, since BM25 and cosine similarity live on incomparable scales. It uses each document's position in each ranked list instead, so a sensible fusion needs no score normalization.

questions.prompt: In which scenario is hybrid search least likely to be worth its extra complexity?
options: A technical support corpus full of product codes and model numbers
A corpus of pure narrative prose with no codes, IDs, or rare named entities, searched only with paraphrased natural-language queries
A legal corpus full of case numbers and statute citations
An e-commerce catalog full of SKUs
questions.explanation: Hybrid search earns its cost when real queries need exact-token matching that dense retrieval misses. A pure-prose corpus searched only with paraphrased queries has little for BM25 to add, so the second index and fusion step buy little accuracy for real infrastructure cost.

posts.title: Human-in-the-Loop: Checkpoints That Keep Agents in Check
posts.subtitle: Full autonomy is fast until an agent force-pushes to main — risk-tiered checkpoints keep the speed without the blast radius.
posts.summary: Giving an agent tool access and a goal means it will eventually propose an action nobody meant to approve — a deletion, a force-push, a real refund. Human-in-the-loop checkpoints gate risky actions behind explicit approval, using a risk-tiered policy so routine work stays fast while costly or irreversible actions get a human's attention.

slides.title: What Stops an Agent From Running a Command It Shouldn't?
slides.body: Give an agent file access, shell commands, and a goal, and it will eventually propose an action nobody meant to approve — a deletion, a force-push, a real purchase.

slides.title: Autonomy and Blast Radius Scale Together
slides.body: The same tool access that lets an agent get useful work done lets it take destructive, hard-to-reverse, or costly actions — and it can't always tell the difference.
bullets: An agent asked to 'clean up stale branches' can't reliably distinguish a genuinely stale branch from someone's unpushed work-in-progress
A support agent empowered to issue refunds has no inherent sense of what dollar amount should trigger a second opinion
Failures compound: one wrong tool call can trigger a chain of further wrong calls before any human notices

slides.title: Checkpoint the Action, Not the Agent
slides.body: A human-in-the-loop (HITL) checkpoint is a blocking gate: the agent proposes an action, a preview of its effect is shown, and execution pauses until a human approves, denies, or edits it.
bullets: Implemented as a tool call that returns 'pending' until a human response arrives — the agent's loop stops there, not after the fact
Risk-tiered policy: read-only actions run automatically, reversible writes run logged but ungated, irreversible/destructive/costly actions require explicit approval
The checkpoint should show a concrete preview — the diff, the exact command, the dollar amount — not a vague 'approve this step?'

slides.title: Three Autonomy Levels, Three Different Costs
slides.body: No single autonomy level is universally correct — the right choice depends on how reversible and costly the agent's actions actually are.

rows: Highest — no gate on any action
Fast for routine, slower for risky
Low on the actions that matter
Proportional — attention goes where risk is

slides.title: A Coding Agent and a 'git push --force'
slides.body: An agent fixing a failing branch decides the cleanest fix is to force-push over what it thinks are stale commits.
bullets: A risk-tiered policy flags any --force, reset --hard, or history-rewriting git command as a required checkpoint, regardless of how confident the agent is
The checkpoint surfaces the exact command plus a diff of the commits that would be discarded — not a vague 'agent wants to push'
A human sees a teammate's unpushed commits in that diff, denies the push, and redirects the agent to rebase instead — the mistake never reaches the remote

slides.title: The Checkpoint Pattern Has Its Own Failure Modes
slides.body: HITL isn't free insurance — badly designed checkpoints create new risks of their own.
bullets: Alert fatigue: if every trivial action needs approval, reviewers start rubber-stamping without reading the diff — the checkpoint becomes theater
Placement matters: a checkpoint right before execution is too late if the agent already queued several dependent actions assuming the first would be approved
Scope creep: an agent can split one risky action into several individually-low-risk ones that together add up to the same blast radius
Skip HITL for short-lived, fully reversible actions in a sandboxed environment (a scratch branch, a test database) — a gate there mostly adds friction

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: HITL checkpoints block execution until a human approves, denies, or edits a proposed action
Risk-tiered policy keeps routine, reversible work fast while gating destructive or costly actions
A checkpoint only works if it shows a concrete preview — the diff, the command, the amount — not a vague confirmation
Gating everything causes alert fatigue and rubber-stamping, which defeats the purpose of the gate

questions.prompt: In a risk-tiered HITL system, what should determine whether an action needs human approval?
options: Whether the agent itself expresses confidence in the action
The action's cost and reversibility, not the agent's confidence
How long the agent's reasoning trace is
Whether a human happens to be online at that moment
questions.explanation: An agent's confidence says nothing about how bad the outcome is if it's wrong. Risk tiering gates based on the action itself — is it destructive, hard to reverse, or costly — which is the actual variable that determines how much a mistake would cost.

questions.prompt: Why does a vague 'approve this step?' prompt undermine a checkpoint?
options: It is technically more secure than a detailed prompt
Reviewers can't evaluate real risk without seeing the concrete effect — the diff, command, or amount — so they end up rubber-stamping
It makes the agent run slower
Most agent frameworks forbid showing details to reviewers
questions.explanation: A checkpoint is only as good as the information it gives the human. Without a concrete preview, a reviewer has nothing to actually evaluate and will tend to approve by default — which defeats the point of gating the action at all.

questions.prompt: What is a known failure mode of putting a checkpoint on every single agent action?
options: The agent becomes completely unable to take any action
Alert fatigue — reviewers stop reading carefully and start rubber-stamping, so the gate stops catching real risk
It makes the agent more accurate automatically
It removes the need for any logging
questions.explanation: Humans have limited attention. Gating low-risk, routine actions at the same level as destructive ones trains reviewers to click approve without reading — so by the time a genuinely risky action shows up, it gets the same rubber-stamp as everything else.

posts.title: Prompt Caching: Skip Re-Reading What You Already Sent
posts.subtitle: A 1.25x write buys a 10x-20x cheaper read on every repeated token — if your prefix stays byte-identical.
posts.summary: Prompt caching persists the KV state computed for a prompt's prefix so a later request with the same prefix skips recomputing attention for it — cutting cost and time-to-first-token on repeated system prompts, tool schemas, and long documents. It only pays off when requests repeat a byte-identical prefix within the cache's TTL.

slides.title: Why Does Every API Call Re-Read Your Whole Prompt?
slides.body: A long system prompt, tool schema, or document gets reprocessed from token zero on every single request — even when 95% of it never changed.

slides.title: Prefill Cost Scales With Every Token You Send, Every Time
slides.body: Before a model generates its first output token, it runs a full forward pass over the entire input — the 'prefill' phase. That cost doesn't know your system prompt was identical to the last 10,000 calls.
bullets: A support bot with a 3,000-token system prompt + tool schema pays for those 3,000 tokens on every single request
At scale (thousands of requests/day) that's pure duplicate compute — same input, same math, same bill
Latency suffers too: prefill time (time-to-first-token) grows with prompt length

slides.title: Cache the KV State for the Prefix, Reuse It on the Next Call
slides.body: During prefill, each layer computes key/value vectors for every token — the 'KV cache.' Prompt caching persists that KV state after the request ends, keyed by a hash of the prefix.
bullets: The next request's prefix hash is checked against stored entries from earlier calls
A match means attention for those tokens is never recomputed — only the new, variable suffix gets processed
On Claude, the cached prefix covers tools → system → messages, up to the block you mark with cache_control
Matching requires the prefix to be 100% identical, including text and images — one changed character invalidates it

slides.title: Worked Example: A Support Agent at 10,000 Requests/Day
slides.body: Claude Opus 5 base input is $5/MTok. A 3,000-token system prompt + tool schema, called 10,000 times a day, shows the gap plainly.
bullets: No caching: 10,000 x 3,000 tokens x $5/MTok = $150/day just for that static prefix
With caching: one write at 1.25x ($6.25/MTok on a 3,000-token prefix ≈ $0.02) then 9,999 reads at 0.1x base ($0.50/MTok) ≈ $15/day total
Net: roughly a 90% cost cut on the repeated portion, plus a faster time-to-first-token since that prefix skips prefill
The win scales with repetition — a prompt that's never reused just eats the write premium for nothing

slides.title: Not Every Provider Caches the Same Way
slides.body: The mechanism is similar everywhere — skip recompute on a matched prefix — but who controls the cache boundary differs.
bullets: Manual breakpoints give you exact control over what's cached and for how long
Automatic matching needs zero code changes but less control over lifetime
Explicit cache objects suit very large, long-lived contexts reused across many sessions

headers: How the cache boundary is set
rows: Manual cache_control breakpoints, up to 4 per request, 5-min or 1-hour TTL
Automatic prefix matching on long prompts — no manual markers to place
Explicit cache object you create and pay to store, then reference by ID

slides.title: The Cache Only Helps If You Structure the Prompt Right
slides.body: Caching rewards a specific prompt shape: stable content first, variable content last.
bullets: Put system prompt, tool definitions, and few-shot examples first, then the changing user turn last — reversing the order breaks every cache hit
A breakpoint on content that changes every call (like a live timestamp) means the hash never matches, so you pay the write premium every single time
The cache expires on a timer (5 minutes by default on Claude) — a workload that calls the API every 20 minutes never benefits, it only pays extra
Caching doesn't expand what the model can 'remember' — it's still bounded by the same context window, just cheaper to resubmit

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Prompt caching reuses the KV cache for a byte-identical prefix — it's a compute/cost optimization, not new memory
Order your prompt: static instructions and tools first, variable content last, with the breakpoint on the last stable block
It only pays off under repetition within the TTL window — high-volume, shared-prefix workloads win; one-off calls lose the write premium
Check your usage response (cache_creation_input_tokens / cache_read_input_tokens) to confirm hits are actually happening

questions.prompt: What does prompt caching actually reuse between requests?
options: The model's trained weights
The key/value (KV) vectors computed for the matching prefix tokens
The final text output from the previous response
The tokenizer's vocabulary file
questions.explanation: Caching persists the per-layer KV state computed during prefill for the prefix tokens, so attention over them doesn't need to be recomputed. The weights and tokenizer never change, and output text isn't what's stored.

questions.prompt: On Claude, why does editing a single word inside your cached system prompt invalidate the cache for every later request?
options: The cache key is a hash of the entire prefix up to the breakpoint, so any change produces a different hash
The API randomly rotates cache keys every few requests for security
Only the first 100 tokens of the prompt are hashed, and that part never changes
Edited prompts are always routed to a different, uncached model
questions.explanation: The cache entry is keyed by a cumulative hash of everything from the start of the prefix through the marked block. Change any earlier token — even one word — and the hash no longer matches, so the request falls back to a full (paid) cache write.

questions.prompt: A workload calls the Claude API once every 20 minutes using the default cache TTL. What happens if it enables prompt caching?
options: It saves money immediately because writes are always cheaper than no caching
Nothing changes — caching is free to enable and has no downside
It pays the ~1.25x write premium every call and never gets a cache hit, since the 5-minute entry always expires first
The 20-minute gap is automatically extended to keep the cache alive
questions.explanation: The default TTL is 5 minutes, refreshed only on a hit. A 20-minute gap between calls means the entry always expires before the next request arrives, so every call pays the write premium with no offsetting cheap read — a net cost increase over no caching at all.

posts.title: FlashProve: Proof of Which Model Actually Replied
posts.subtitle: A zero-knowledge proof that the model you paid for is the model that answered.
posts.summary: Anthropic's FlashProve generates a succinct cryptographic proof that a specific committed model produced a specific reply, without revealing the weights. It proves a 400B-parameter MoE model at ~110 tokens/second, about 70-95x slower than plain inference but far faster than any prior open zkML system.

slides.title: Can You Prove Which Model Answered You?
slides.body: Anthropic's Frontier Red Team built a cryptographic proof system that answers that question for a 400B-parameter model, without showing anyone the weights.

slides.title: Judging the Output Isn't Enough
slides.body: A provider could quietly swap a cheap model into an expensive model's slot, or a compromised server could run tampered weights. Reading the reply can't catch that.
bullets: Pacing: regulators need proof compute went to inference, not secret training
Tamper detection: operators need proof the right weights ran on the right server
Text provenance: users need proof a specific model wrote a specific answer
Model approval: regulators may require only approved models be served

slides.title: Commit, Prove, Verify
slides.body: FlashProve is a zkSNARK for Mixture-of-Experts models, built in two phases so most of the cost happens once, not per request.
bullets: Offline: the provider publishes a short commitment (fingerprint) to the weights — one commitment covers ~16M requests
Online: for each reply, the prover produces a proof that the committed model, on this prompt, outputs these exact tokens
Properties proved in Lean 4: completeness, soundness, zero-knowledge, succinctness
Security rests only on standard hash functions (SHA-256/SHA-3) — no elliptic curves, no trusted setup

slides.title: Why It's Fast Enough to Matter
slides.body: The trick is proving only what actually ran.
bullets: Prover cost scales with active parameters per token (~17B), not the full model (~400B)
Requests are proved in batches after generation, like a parallel prefill pass
Weights stream in layer segments, so one 80GB H100 + ~290GB host RAM suffices
Verifying is mostly hashing — a CPU checks a proof in ~17 seconds on 24 threads

slides.title: Every Prior zkML System Was Too Slow to Ship
slides.body: Same-model comparison: proving Llama 4 Maverick (400B total, 17B active) in different systems.

slides.title: What One Proof Actually Costs
slides.body: Concrete numbers from the paper's benchmark run, one H100 GPU, 24 CPU cores.
bullets: Offline commitment: ~39 minutes, once, before serving any traffic
Online: a batch of 24 requests takes ~223 seconds to prove — about 110 tok/s
Each proof is ~18.78MB; the commitment anyone downloads is only ~6.5MB
Overhead vs. plain vLLM (FP8, 8x H100): ~72-94x slower per GPU, depending on load

slides.title: Where It Breaks Down — Read the Fine Print
slides.body: This is a research prototype, not a drop-in guarantee.
bullets: 70-95x compute overhead rules out latency-critical, high-margin serving today
Proofs cover exact integer weights and greedy decoding only — not sampling or float outputs
Context window capped at 1,024 tokens per proof, far short of real deployments
Architecture (MoE, layer shapes) is NOT hidden — only the weight values are
A proof shows hardware served inference; it can't rule out training happening on the side

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: FlashProve proves "this exact committed model produced this exact reply" — cryptographically, not by trust
~110 tok/s and 19MB proofs make it the fastest open zkML system for a frontier-scale MoE model by a wide margin
The 70-95x overhead means this is a trust primitive for audits and compliance today, not a default inference mode
Code, Lean proofs, and a C++ verifier are open-sourced (Apache 2.0) at anthropics/FlashProve

questions.prompt: What does FlashProve's zero-knowledge property actually hide?
options: The model's architecture, including that it's a Mixture-of-Experts model
The weight values and intermediate computation, while the architecture stays visible
Which GPU the proof was generated on
The prompt the user submitted
questions.explanation: The paper is explicit: zero-knowledge covers weights and intermediate values (and which experts fired), but the MoE architecture itself is not hidden — hiding architecture too is listed as future work.

questions.prompt: Roughly how much slower is FlashProve than plain vLLM inference on the same model?
options: About 2x slower
About 10x slower
About 70-95x slower
About 1000x slower
questions.explanation: Proving a batch of 24 requests took roughly 66-94x longer per GPU than plain vLLM (FP8, 8xH100) across the tested load range — fast for a zkML system, but still nowhere near free.

questions.prompt: Why can FlashProve prove a 400B-parameter model without the prover cost exploding?
options: It skips proving most tokens and samples a few at random
It only proves work proportional to the ~17B active parameters per token, not the full 400B
It runs the proof entirely on CPU, which is cheaper than GPU
It compresses the model to a smaller size before proving
questions.explanation: Because the model is Mixture-of-Experts, each token only activates ~17B of the 400B total parameters — and FlashProve's prover cost scales with that active count, not the full model size.
