posts.title: Mixture of Experts: Routing Tokens to Specialists
posts.subtitle: How a 400B-parameter model answers using only 17B parameters per token.
posts.summary: Mixture of Experts (MoE) swaps a model's dense feed-forward layer for many smaller expert networks and a router that picks a handful per token. It's how frontier models get bigger without getting proportionally slower — at the cost of load-balancing headaches and no memory savings.

slides.title: Bigger Models Without Bigger Bills
slides.body: Dense models pay full compute for every parameter, on every token. Mixture of Experts breaks that link.

slides.title: Dense Models Scale Compute 1:1 With Parameters
slides.body: In a dense transformer, every token passes through every weight in every feed-forward layer. Double the parameters, double the FLOPs per token — there's no way to add knowledge without adding latency.
bullets: A dense 400B model spends 400B-parameters worth of compute on every single token
Most of that capacity is irrelevant to any given token — you rarely need all of it at once
This is the wall that made "just add more parameters" expensive to keep doing

slides.title: Split the FFN Into Experts, Add a Router
slides.body: MoE replaces one big feed-forward block with N smaller "expert" FFNs plus a tiny router network.
bullets: The router scores every expert for each token (a softmax over N logits)
Only the top-k experts (commonly k=1 or k=2) actually run for that token
The token's output is the weighted sum of just those experts' outputs
Attention layers usually stay dense — only the FFN is sparsified

slides.title: Total Parameters vs. Active Parameters
slides.body: What actually fires per token varies a lot by model.

slides.title: Experts Don't Specialize the Way You'd Guess
slides.body: It's tempting to picture a "biology expert" and a "math expert." Studies of trained MoE routers (e.g. Mixtral's analysis) found something messier.
bullets: Routing correlates more with syntax and token position than with topic or subject matter
The same expert often fires for a token regardless of the surrounding sentence's domain
Specialization exists, but it's statistical and distributed — not a clean subject-matter split
This matters for debugging: you can't just ask "which expert knows chemistry?"

slides.title: The Catch: Memory Doesn't Shrink, and Routing Can Collapse
slides.body: MoE buys you compute efficiency, not the savings people assume.
bullets: ALL experts must stay loaded in memory — a 671B MoE still needs 671B worth of VRAM/storage
Naive training can route everything to a few popular experts, starving the rest ("routing collapse")
Fix: an auxiliary load-balancing loss penalizes uneven expert usage during training
At inference, all-to-all communication between GPUs (to ship tokens to their experts) adds real network overhead at scale
Not worth it below a certain scale — the routing and balancing overhead can cost more than it saves on small models

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: MoE decouples total knowledge (parameter count) from per-token compute cost — that's the entire trade
Top-k routing (usually k=1 or k=2) picks a handful of experts per token from a much larger pool
It saves compute and latency, not memory — every expert still has to be loaded somewhere
Load balancing is the hard engineering problem, not the routing math itself

questions.prompt: What does Mixture of Experts primarily save, compared to a dense model of the same total size?
options: GPU memory needed to hold the model
Compute (FLOPs) spent per token
The size of the model on disk
The number of training tokens needed
questions.explanation: MoE only runs the top-k selected experts per token, so compute per token scales with active parameters, not total parameters. Memory still has to hold every expert, so it doesn't shrink.

questions.prompt: What is "routing collapse" in an MoE model?
options: The router crashing due to a software bug
Training pushing most tokens to a few popular experts while others go unused
The model running out of GPU memory mid-inference
Experts disagreeing on the output for a token
questions.explanation: Without a balancing mechanism, gradient dynamics can funnel traffic into a small set of experts, which both wastes capacity and overloads those experts — the usual fix is an auxiliary load-balancing loss during training.

questions.prompt: Based on real MoE routing studies, what do experts actually tend to specialize in?
options: Clean subject-matter domains, like one expert per academic field
Mostly syntax and token position rather than topic
Nothing — routing is effectively random
The language the input text is written in
questions.explanation: Analyses of trained routers (e.g. on Mixtral) found routing correlates more with surface features like syntax and position than with subject domain — the "one expert per topic" mental model is a simplification.

posts.title: Tool Calling: How LLMs Actually Invoke Functions
posts.subtitle: The model never runs code — it emits a structured request and waits.
posts.summary: Tool calling lets an LLM request a real action instead of guessing at one in prose: the model emits a structured call matching a JSON Schema, your code executes it, and the result goes back into the conversation. The protocol is simple; the failure modes — tool sprawl, untrusted arguments, non-idempotent side effects — are where real systems break.

slides.body: Every agent framework — from a weekend script to a production fleet — reduces to this one loop.
slides.title: Tool Calling: How LLMs Actually Invoke Functions

bullets: No guarantee the model picks a real function name
No guarantee arguments are well-typed or complete
No clean way to feed a result back into reasoning
slides.body: Ask a model to 'call the weather API' in plain prose and you get prose back — maybe a fake city name, maybe malformed JSON, maybe a confident hallucinated response with no API call at all.
slides.title: Free text can't safely touch the real world

bullets: 1. You attach tool schemas to the request
2. Model emits a tool-call block instead of (or alongside) prose
3. Your code validates args and executes the real function
4. The result is appended as a tool-result message; model continues
slides.body: You send tool definitions (name, description, JSON Schema for parameters) alongside the conversation. The model doesn't run anything — it emits a structured block naming a tool and its arguments.
slides.title: The loop: declare, decide, execute, return

bullets: Structural validity is enforced during decoding, not just checked after
Modern APIs allow several tool-call blocks in one turn, run concurrently
The conversation becomes a typed sequence: user → tool_use → tool_result → assistant
slides.body: Many runtimes don't just validate the JSON after the fact — they grammar-constrain token sampling so the model literally cannot emit a key or type the schema disallows.
slides.title: Schemas constrain more than they describe

bullets: Model emits two parallel tool calls instead of guessing an answer
Your code runs both, returns {temp: 14, condition: 'rain'} and a flight list
Model synthesizes: 'Rainy and $420 round-trip — maybe wait for next week'
Without tool calling, the model would have invented a plausible-sounding forecast
slides.body: An agent holds two tools: get_weather(city) and search_flights(origin, destination, date).
slides.title: Worked example: 'Should I fly to Lisbon this weekend?'

rows: Typed tool_use / tool_calls block in the API response
Model writes 'Action: search("x")' as plain text
Token sampling masked to match the JSON Schema

slides.title: Not every implementation is native

bullets: Tool sprawl: past ~20-30 similarly-named tools, selection accuracy drops
Untrusted input: model-authored arguments are attacker-reachable if any tool output came from the open web — validate server-side, never trust blindly
Non-idempotent tools (send_email, charge_card) need explicit idempotency keys — a retried call must not double-fire
Skip tool calling for facts the model already knows well; a tool round-trip adds latency for no benefit
slides.title: Where it breaks in production

bullets: The model only ever proposes a call — your code is the one actually executing it
JSON Schema is enforced, not just suggested — many runtimes constrain sampling to match it
Parallel tool calls let one turn gather several results before replying
Guard non-idempotent tools and validate arguments like any other untrusted input
slides.title: Takeaways

questions.prompt: When an LLM 'calls a tool', what does it actually emit?
options: Executable code that runs inside the model
A structured block naming the tool and arguments matching its schema
A raw shell command
Nothing — the host executes automatically without any model output
questions.explanation: The model never executes anything itself. It emits a structured request (tool name + arguments); your application code is what actually performs the real action and returns a result.

questions.prompt: Why attach a JSON Schema to a tool instead of just describing it in a sentence?
options: It's required by the HTTP spec
It always reduces token usage
It structurally constrains and validates the arguments the model can produce
It makes the tool run faster
questions.explanation: A schema gives the runtime something to enforce — many implementations constrain token sampling so the model can't emit a field or type the schema disallows, catching errors before execution rather than after.

questions.prompt: An agent is given 50 overlapping tools. What's the most likely failure mode?
options: Tool calling stops working entirely above 10 tools
The model always picks the alphabetically first tool
Selection accuracy drops as the model confuses similarly-named or overlapping tools
Nothing changes — tool count never affects behavior
questions.explanation: Tool selection is itself a reasoning step. Past roughly 20-30 similar tools, models increasingly pick the wrong one or miss the right one — grouping or hierarchically routing tools helps.

posts.title: MCP Primitives: Who Decides — Model, App, or User?
posts.subtitle: Tools, Resources, and Prompts aren't three names for the same thing.
posts.summary: MCP gives servers three distinct ways to expose capability to a client: Tools (the model decides to call them), Resources (the host app decides to attach them), and Prompts (the user decides to invoke them). Collapsing all three into 'just a tool' is the most common MCP design mistake.

slides.body: Model Context Protocol isn't just a function-calling standard. It has three primitives, and each hands control to someone different.
slides.title: MCP Primitives: Who Decides — Model, App, or User?

bullets: A model-invoked action and a host-attached file need different safeguards
Without a shared vocabulary, every integration re-solves the same design problem
slides.body: One agent framework treats everything as a function. Another treats everything as a document. Neither distinguishes 'the model chose this' from 'the app attached this' from 'the user asked for this' — yet those are very different trust boundaries.
slides.title: Before MCP, every framework invented its own object model

bullets: Tools — model-controlled: name + description + JSON Schema input; the model decides when to call one, same shape as classic function calling
Resources — application-controlled: context identified by a URI (file://, postgres://, custom schemes); the host lists/reads/subscribes to them, the model doesn't fetch them itself
Prompts — user-controlled: parameterized templates the server exposes, typically surfaced as discoverable slash-commands in the client UI
slides.title: The three primitives, by who controls them

bullets: Client and server negotiate capabilities during the initialize handshake — which of tools/resources/prompts each side supports
list_tools / list_resources / list_prompts: discovery
call_tool / read_resource / get_prompt: invocation
Resources can optionally be subscribed to, so the server pushes update notifications instead of the host re-polling
slides.title: Discovery and invocation are separate calls

bullets: Tool: create_pull_request(schema) — model decides to call it after reasoning about a change
Resource: repo://owner/repo/file/path.py — host reads file content on demand, outside the model's control
Prompt: /review-pr — user types it with a PR number; server returns a filled-in review template as a ready-made user message
Sequence: user runs /review-pr 482 → client calls get_prompt → template is sent as a message → model reads the repo:// resource the host attached → model then calls the create_pull_request tool
slides.title: Worked example: a GitHub MCP server

rows: A GET request or file read

slides.title: Same protocol, three different trust boundaries

bullets: Exposing a large file as a Tool result dumps it straight into the model's context on every call — it should be a Resource the host can paginate, cache, or summarize first
Most shipped servers implement Tools only; Resources and Prompts are frequently skipped even though they fit the data better
Client support varies — not every MCP host renders Prompts as UI menu items or supports Resource subscriptions, so the same server can feel different across apps
slides.title: Where MCP servers go wrong

bullets: Tools, Resources, and Prompts map to three different deciders: model, app, user
Putting everything behind Tools forces model-token cost onto data that should be host-managed
Capability negotiation at initialize is what lets a client and server agree what's even available
Check which primitives your MCP client actually renders — a feature-complete server can look incomplete in a client that ignores Resources or Prompts
slides.title: Takeaways

questions.prompt: Which MCP primitive is invoked by the model itself, without a human explicitly choosing to use it?
options: Resources
Prompts
Tools
None — all three require user action
questions.explanation: Tools are the model-controlled primitive, functionally equivalent to classic function calling. Resources are attached by the host application, and Prompts are triggered by the user.

questions.prompt: Why expose a large file as an MCP Resource instead of returning it from a Tool call?
options: Resources are faster over the network
Resources let the host control when and how much enters the model's context, instead of dumping the full content on every tool call
Tools can't return large payloads at all
There's no difference — it's a naming convention only
questions.explanation: A Resource is application-controlled: the host can paginate, cache, or summarize it before anything reaches the model. A Tool result goes straight into the model's token budget every single call.

questions.prompt: What must a client and server agree on before any tools/resources/prompts calls can happen?
options: Nothing — any call can be attempted at any time
A shared API key
Which capabilities each side supports, negotiated during the initialize handshake
The exact UI the client will use to render results
questions.explanation: MCP sessions begin with a capability negotiation: client and server each declare which primitives (tools, resources, prompts, sampling) they support, so later calls only target what's actually available.

posts.title: Test-Time Compute: Thinking Longer Instead of Scaling Up
posts.subtitle: Why letting a model deliberate longer at answer time can beat training a bigger one
posts.summary: Test-time compute (inference-time scaling) lets a model spend extra computation at answer time — longer reasoning chains, multiple sampled attempts, or self-revision — instead of only scaling up parameters and training data. For verifiable, reasoning-heavy tasks like math and code this often buys more accuracy per dollar than training a larger model, but it trades latency and per-query cost for that accuracy, and it does nothing for tasks where the model's knowledge, not its reasoning, is the bottleneck.

slides.title: A Third Dial Beyond Bigger Models and More Data
slides.body: For years, making an LLM smarter meant one of two things: more parameters, or more training data. Test-time compute adds a third dial — spend more computation after training, while the model is actually answering a question.
bullets: Also called inference-time scaling, or 'reasoning compute'
Popularized by reasoning models that visibly deliberate before answering

slides.title: Train-Time Scaling Is Hitting Diminishing Returns
slides.body: Classic scaling laws say accuracy improves predictably as you add parameters and data — but each meaningful jump costs a roughly proportional jump in training compute, and high-quality training data is finite.
bullets: A 10x bigger training run doesn't produce a model that's reliably 10x better at hard reasoning
Most of that extra capacity goes to broad knowledge a specific task doesn't need
A fixed-size model can still fail a hard reasoning problem it 'knows enough' to solve — it just doesn't deliberate before answering

slides.title: Let the Model Spend Tokens Deliberating, Not Just Answering
slides.body: Instead of emitting an answer immediately, the model generates intermediate reasoning tokens — a scratchpad — before committing to a final answer. Using more of that scratchpad well acts like buying more thinking time.
bullets: Longer chain-of-thought: reason step-by-step across more tokens before answering
Best-of-N sampling: generate N independent attempts, then pick the best via a verifier or a vote
Self-revision: draft an answer, critique it, and revise — sometimes across several passes

slides.title: How a Verifier Turns Many Attempts Into One Good Answer
slides.body: Sampling N candidate solutions only helps if something can tell good from bad. That job falls to a verifier — a scoring pass, a learned reward model, or a simple vote.
bullets: Self-consistency: sample N chains-of-thought, take the majority final answer — works when errors are random rather than systematic
Learned verifiers: a reward model scores each candidate and the system keeps the top-scoring one
Process supervision: reward correct intermediate reasoning steps, not just the final answer, catching mistakes before they compound

slides.title: Train-Time Scaling vs. Test-Time Scaling
slides.body: They aren't competitors so much as two different places to spend compute, with very different cost profiles.

slides.title: Worked Example: A Hard Multi-Step Math Problem
slides.body: Give a reasoning-capable model a multi-step competition math problem and compare two settings.
bullets: Minimal-reasoning mode: the model pattern-matches to a similar-looking problem and answers confidently — and wrongly
Extended-reasoning mode: it sets up the problem, tries an approach, notices a contradiction mid-chain, backtracks, and retries with a different method
Sampling 8 independent attempts and taking the majority answer catches the case where one chain goes off the rails but most don't
The same underlying model gets meaningfully more problems right purely by being allowed to spend more tokens per answer

slides.title: When Test-Time Compute Doesn't Help — or Actively Hurts
slides.body: Extra deliberation only pays off where the bottleneck is reasoning, not knowledge.
bullets: Factual lookup tasks: no amount of extra thinking recovers a fact the model never learned — that's a retrieval problem, not a reasoning one
Cost multiplies fast: sampling 8-32 candidates for verification means roughly 8-32x the inference cost, often for a shrinking accuracy gain past a point
Diminishing returns: accuracy on reasoning benchmarks tends to flatten once enough reasoning tokens are used — doubling compute again rarely doubles the gain
Latency-sensitive products (autocomplete, voice assistants) often can't absorb the extra seconds a long reasoning chain adds

slides.title: What to Remember
slides.body: Test-time compute is a genuine third axis for improving LLM performance — complementary to, not a replacement for, bigger and better-trained models.
bullets: Reasoning-heavy, verifiable tasks (math, code, logic puzzles) benefit the most
The gain is bought with latency and per-query cost — budget for both before turning it on
The verification method matters as much as the extra compute: more tokens with no way to pick the best answer wastes the budget
For knowledge-bound tasks, better retrieval or a bigger model beats a longer reasoning chain every time

questions.prompt: What makes 'self-consistency' sampling work as a test-time compute technique?
options: It fine-tunes the model's weights on each new question before answering
It samples multiple independent reasoning chains and takes the majority final answer, which cancels out random, non-systematic errors
It always samples exactly two attempts and averages their numeric outputs
It replaces the model's training data with synthetic reasoning traces
questions.explanation: Self-consistency works because sampling errors are often random rather than systematic — if most independent chains reach the same answer, that answer is more likely correct. It fails when the model has a systematic blind spot, since every sample would share the same mistake.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't test-time compute help a model answer a question about a fact it was never trained on?
options: Extended reasoning only re-orders existing knowledge and reasoning steps — it can't recover information the model never learned
Test-time compute always reduces the model's effective context window
Reasoning tokens are stripped out before the model sees the question
Fact-based questions are rejected by the tokenizer
questions.explanation: Test-time compute spends more tokens deliberating over what the model already knows — it's a reasoning amplifier, not a knowledge source. A missing fact is a retrieval or training-data problem, not something a longer chain-of-thought can fix.

questions.prompt: What's the main cost trade-off when turning up test-time compute, e.g. sampling 16 candidates instead of 1?
options: It has no effect on cost since the number of parameters stays the same
Inference cost and often latency scale roughly with the number of candidates or reasoning tokens, while accuracy gains tend to flatten past a point
It reduces inference cost because the model needs fewer parameters
It only affects training cost, not inference
questions.explanation: Each extra sampled attempt or reasoning token is paid for on every single query, unlike training compute which is paid once — so cost and latency scale with how much test-time compute is used, even as the accuracy curve flattens.

posts.title: Context Engineering: Curating What the Model Sees
posts.subtitle: The discipline of keeping an agent's context window full of signal, not noise
posts.summary: Context engineering is the practice of curating every token an LLM sees at inference — not just the prompt, but tools, retrieved data, and history — down to the smallest high-signal set. It matters because 'context rot' makes models quietly less reliable as their window fills up, and the fix is picking the right technique (compaction, note-taking, or sub-agents) for the task at hand.

slides.title: The Hardest Part of Agents Isn't the Prompt — It's the Context
slides.body: Anthropic's engineering team coined 'context engineering' to describe something bigger than prompt wording: curating the entire set of tokens — system instructions, tools, retrieved data, message history — that an agent sees on every single inference call.
bullets: It's iterative — curation happens on every call, not once at the start
Goal: the smallest possible set of high-signal tokens that makes the right outcome likely

slides.title: Context Rot: More Tokens, Quietly Worse Recall
slides.body: As a context window fills up, a model's ability to recall and use any single piece of it degrades — gradually, not as a sudden cliff, which is exactly why teams miss it until an agent is well into a long session.
bullets: Attention is pairwise across every token (n² relationships) — longer contexts stretch the same attention budget thinner
Models are trained on far fewer long sequences than short ones, so long-range recall is inherently weaker
Position-encoding interpolation lets models accept longer inputs, but blurs precise positional information

slides.title: Three Places the Token Budget Gets Spent — and Wasted
slides.body: Context engineering starts with the pieces you control before any retrieval happens: the system prompt, the tool definitions, and the examples.
bullets: System prompts: aim for the 'right altitude' — not brittle hardcoded if/else, not vague platitudes either
Tools: keep them self-contained, error-tolerant, minimally overlapping, and token-efficient in what they return
Examples: a handful of diverse, canonical few-shot examples beats a long list of edge-case rules

slides.title: Two Ways Data Gets Into the Window: Upfront or Just-in-Time
slides.body: Classic RAG retrieves and injects before the model runs. The alternative — just-in-time retrieval — has the agent keep lightweight references and pull data at runtime.
bullets: Just-in-time: the agent holds file paths or stored queries, then loads data on demand with tools
Claude Code uses this for large datasets — inspecting results the way a terminal 'head' or 'tail' would, instead of loading everything
Hybrid: load a little upfront (e.g. a CLAUDE.md file) and explore the rest on demand — suits less dynamic domains like legal or finance
Trade-off: runtime exploration is slower, and wastes context outright if the agent chases dead ends

slides.title: Worked Example: A Research Agent That Would Blow Its Budget
slides.body: A lead agent needs to synthesize findings from dozens of sources. Letting it read everything directly would flood its own context long before it starts writing.
bullets: Instead, specialized sub-agents each get a clean context window and can burn 10,000+ tokens scanning sources
Each sub-agent returns only a condensed summary to the lead agent — roughly 1,000–2,000 tokens
The lead agent never sees the raw exploration, only the distillation — its own window stays focused
Anthropic reports this multi-agent pattern beats single-agent setups by a wide margin on complex research tasks, at the cost of more total tokens spent across all sub-agents combined

slides.title: Three Techniques for Tasks That Outlive One Context Window
slides.body: Long-horizon agent work (minutes to hours) needs a strategy for what happens when the window fills up.

rows: Summarize the conversation near the limit, restart with the summary
Agent writes persistent notes (e.g. a NOTES.md) outside the window, reloads them later
Specialized agents explore in isolated context, return condensed summaries
Research that benefits from parallel exploration

slides.title: Where Context Engineering Goes Wrong
slides.body: The techniques above are easy to misapply — and misapplying them can make an agent worse, not better.
bullets: Over-compacting: summarizing too aggressively drops the one detail — an unresolved bug, a key decision — the agent needed later; tune for recall first, precision second
Bloated tool sets: overlapping tools create ambiguous choices that burn tokens on indecision instead of progress
'Just add more RAG' as a reflex: most context problems are signal-to-noise, not recall — pouring more retrieved text into an already-crowded window deepens context rot
Skip all of this for short, single-turn tasks — if the whole job fits comfortably in one window, the retrieval/compaction pipeline is pure overhead

slides.title: What to Remember
slides.body: Context engineering treats the window as a finite, precious resource — not a place to dump everything that might be relevant.
bullets: Every token competes for the same attention budget — bigger isn't safer
The goal is the smallest high-signal set, not the largest possible one
Match the technique to the task: compaction for long chats, notes for iterative work, sub-agents for parallel research
Smarter models need less prescriptive engineering, but 'do the simplest thing that works' still wins

questions.prompt: What does 'context rot' describe?
options: Tokens becoming corrupted when a context window is stored to disk
A model's recall accuracy gradually declining as more tokens fill its context window
Context windows shrinking with each new model release
Tool outputs going stale after an API changes
questions.explanation: Context rot is the gradual decline in a model's ability to recall and use information as its context window fills up. It's gradual rather than a sharp cliff, which is why teams often don't notice it until a long-running agent starts quietly missing details.

questions.prompt: In the sub-agent pattern, roughly how much does a sub-agent condense its findings before handing them to the lead agent?
options: From a few hundred tokens down to a single word
From tens of thousands of tokens of exploration down to roughly 1,000–2,000 tokens
It passes its entire context window along unmodified
It returns only a true/false success flag
questions.explanation: Sub-agents work in their own clean context windows — spending tens of thousands of tokens if needed — then return a condensed summary of roughly 1,000–2,000 tokens, so the lead agent's window stays focused on synthesis rather than raw exploration.

questions.prompt: Why can 'just add more RAG' make an agent's context problems worse instead of better?
options: RAG retrieval is always too slow to be useful in production
Most context problems come from low signal-to-noise ratio, not insufficient recall, so adding more retrieved text to an already-crowded window deepens context rot
Vector databases cannot index more than a few thousand documents
RAG systems cannot be combined with tool use
questions.explanation: When an agent is struggling, the instinct is often to retrieve more. But if the real problem is that the window is already full of low-signal tokens, adding more retrieved text just dilutes attention further — the fix is better curation, not more volume.

posts.title: HNSW: How Vector Databases Find Nearest Neighbors Fast
posts.subtitle: Multi-layer graphs that turn billion-vector search into millisecond lookups
posts.summary: HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) is the graph structure behind most vector databases. It trades a small amount of recall for a huge speedup over brute-force search by letting queries 'zoom in' through layers of shortcuts instead of checking every vector. Knowing its M and ef_search knobs — and when NOT to reach for it — is core RAG infrastructure literacy.

slides.title: 50 Million Vectors. Find the 10 Closest. In Milliseconds.
slides.body: That's the job every RAG system hands to its vector index on every single query. Doing it naively doesn't scale — doing it with HNSW is why 'semantic search' feels instant.
bullets: Powers Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, pgvector, FAISS
Approximate, not exact — and that's the whole point

slides.title: Brute-Force Search Is Linear — and Linear Doesn't Scale
slides.body: Exact nearest-neighbor search compares the query against every stored vector. The cost grows directly with how many vectors you have, which is fine at 10K and brutal at 50M.
bullets: 10M vectors × 768 dimensions ≈ billions of multiply-adds per single query
Cost is O(n·d): double your corpus, double the latency
No amount of better hardware fixes an algorithm that's fundamentally O(n)

slides.title: HNSW Builds a Highway System, Not a Flat List
slides.body: HNSW organizes vectors into stacked graph layers. The top layer has few nodes with long-range links (highways); each layer down gets denser with shorter links, until the bottom layer holds every vector.
bullets: Search starts at the sparse top layer and greedily hops toward the query
Each layer narrows the search before dropping to the next, denser one
Query cost becomes roughly O(log n) instead of O(n) — exponentially cheaper at scale

slides.title: Two Knobs Control the Speed/Accuracy Trade
slides.body: HNSW exposes build-time and query-time parameters that trade memory and latency for recall.
bullets: M: max edges per node at build time — higher M means a denser graph, better recall, more RAM
ef_construction: how hard the graph tries to find good neighbors while building — higher is slower to build, higher quality
ef_search: how many candidates to explore per query — higher means slower queries but closer to the true top-k
Typical defaults: M≈16, ef_construction≈200 — tuned up for recall-sensitive workloads, down for raw speed

slides.title: HNSW vs. the Alternatives
slides.body: Every ANN index picks a different point on the same speed/memory/recall triangle.

rows: Highest — graph edges roughly double vector storage

slides.title: Worked Example: A RAG Chatbot Over 5M Document Chunks
slides.body: A support bot embeds 5M chunks once at index time. At query time, it embeds the user's question and asks the index for the 8 closest chunks to feed the LLM.
bullets: Without HNSW: compare the query to all 5M chunks — seconds of latency, dead on arrival for a chat UI
With HNSW: entry from the top layer lands near the right neighborhood in a handful of hops
Each layer re-ranks a shrinking candidate set until the bottom layer returns the true nearest chunks
Typical result: sub-50ms retrieval even as the corpus grows into the tens of millions

slides.title: When NOT to Reach for HNSW
slides.body: HNSW is not free, and it's the wrong tool for some very common situations.
bullets: Frequent deletes/updates are awkward — nodes are usually tombstoned, not cleanly removed, so the graph degrades and needs periodic rebuilds
Build time is nontrivial — inserting millions of vectors one-by-one is far slower than a flat index
Small corpora (under ~100K vectors) often don't need it — brute-force on modern hardware can be fast enough, and it's exact
Memory-constrained environments may prefer IVF or product quantization, since HNSW's graph edges cost real RAM

slides.title: What to Remember
slides.body: HNSW is the default choice for most RAG vector search, not because it's exact, but because it's a well-tuned trade.
bullets: It replaces O(n) brute-force search with roughly O(log n) graph traversal
M and ef_search are your levers — tune them per workload instead of trusting defaults blindly
It's approximate by design: measure recall@k on your own data before trusting it in production
Skip it for tiny corpora or write-heavy workloads — brute-force or IVF may serve you better there

questions.prompt: Why does HNSW search start at the top graph layer instead of the bottom?
options: The top layer is sparse with long-range links, so it quickly narrows the search region before descending to denser layers
The top layer contains the most recently inserted vectors
The bottom layer is reserved for deleted vectors
Starting at the top avoids needing an ef_search parameter
questions.explanation: HNSW's layers mirror a skip-list: the top has few, long-range edges ('highways'), so a few hops there get you close to the answer before finer-grained layers refine it — that's what makes the search roughly O(log n).

questions.prompt: You raise ef_search from 50 to 200 on an existing HNSW index. What's the most likely effect?
options: The index needs to be rebuilt from scratch
Recall improves and query latency increases, since more candidates are explored per search
Memory usage roughly doubles
Nothing changes — ef_search only affects index construction
questions.explanation: ef_search is a query-time knob: a higher value explores more candidates before returning results, which generally improves recall at the cost of slower queries. It doesn't require a rebuild or change memory footprint.

questions.prompt: A team has 40,000 product embeddings that get updated constantly throughout the day. Why might HNSW be a poor fit?
options: HNSW only supports embeddings under 128 dimensions
HNSW requires a GPU to build the graph
At that scale brute-force is already fast and exact, while HNSW's graph degrades under frequent updates and needs periodic rebuilding
HNSW cannot return more than 10 results per query
questions.explanation: 40K vectors is small enough that exact brute-force search is often fast enough in practice — and HNSW adds real cost here: deletes are usually tombstoned rather than removed, so a write-heavy workload degrades the graph and forces periodic rebuilds.

posts.title: MANDATE: Mapping 23 Ways AI Agents Fail Their Users
posts.subtitle: Microsoft and Georgia Tech mined 163K Reddit posts to find why delegation breaks trust
posts.summary: A new paper from Microsoft and Georgia Tech mined 163,487 Reddit posts to build MANDATE, a 23-category taxonomy of how AI agents fail the people delegating to them. The core finding: task completion and user trust are different axes entirely — an agent can finish the job and still violate what the user expected, and the worst failures are often the hardest to notice.

slides.title: What If Your Agent Finishes the Task — and Still Breaks Your Trust?
slides.body: Most agent benchmarks measure one thing: did it complete the task. A new study says that's the wrong lens entirely.
bullets: 163,487 Reddit posts analyzed
23 failure categories across 7 groups

slides.title: Benchmarks Measure Success. Users Experience Something Else.
slides.body: "Babysitting AI Agents: A User-Centered Taxonomy and Study of Agentic Delegation Failures" (Mittal et al., Microsoft & Georgia Tech, arXiv 2610.34748) argues that agent evaluation has a blind spot: task completion rates say nothing about whether the way a task got done matched what the user actually expected.
bullets: Agentic delegation failure: when an agent's process departs from a user's expectations, independent of whether the end result was technically correct
Existing red-teaming taxonomies focus on safety failures, not everyday trust-eroding ones
The authors went straight to real users instead of lab benchmarks: 163,487 Reddit posts describing real-world AI agent use

slides.title: Building MANDATE: A Taxonomy Mined From the Wild
slides.body: The team built an LLM-based classification pipeline rather than hand-coding every category from scratch.
bullets: Step 1: classify whether each Reddit post describes a delegation failure at all
Step 2: for posts that do, classify which of 23 failure categories (grouped into 7 higher-level groups) it falls into
Pipeline surfaced 6,623 concrete failure instances out of the full 163,487-post corpus
Authors: Shravika Mittal, Sunnie S. Y. Kim, Scott Counts, Jennifer Neville, Debarati Das, and Philippe Laban

slides.title: Then They Tested It on 73 Real Agent Users
slides.body: A taxonomy built from text posts is only useful if it maps onto how people actually perceive failures, so the team ran a follow-up user study.
bullets: 73 experienced agent users were shown real failure scenarios drawn from the taxonomy
Each participant rated scenarios on perceived severity and how easy the failure was to notice
Prior personal experience with a given failure type was tracked as a variable, not assumed away

slides.title: The Core Finding: Severity and Visibility Pull in Opposite Directions
slides.body: The study's headline result isn't a new failure mode — it's a pattern across all of them.
bullets: Failures rated more severe by users were also rated harder to notice in the moment
Having previously experienced a failure type made it noticeably easier to spot the next time
Net effect: the failures that matter most are structurally the ones users are worst-equipped to catch

slides.title: The Blind Spot the Paper Calls Out by Name
slides.body: The authors explicitly flag which failures are common in the wild but barely studied in agent research — a concrete, low-drama example: agents that run without making any progress.
bullets: An agent loops, re-plans, or retries indefinitely — burning time and tokens without advancing the task
It isn't a crash and it isn't a wrong answer, so it rarely trips alarms in standard evaluations
A user has to notice the agent is 'busy but going nowhere' entirely on their own, often only after wasted cost
This is exactly the kind of failure the severity/noticeability finding predicts users will catch late

slides.title: What the Paper Doesn't Settle
slides.body: The authors' own setup has real limits worth keeping in mind before generalizing too far.
bullets: Classification into categories relied on an LLM classifier, which can mislabel edge cases the way any automated pipeline can
The corpus is self-selected Reddit posters describing their own experience — not a random sample of all agent users
73 participants is enough to find a pattern, not enough to say how it varies across agent types, tasks, or user expertise

slides.title: What Builders Should Take From This
slides.body: If you're shipping an agent, task success rate is necessary but not sufficient.
bullets: 163,487 posts → 6,623 real failure instances → 23 categories across 7 groups (the MANDATE taxonomy)
Design for process transparency, not just outcome correctness — show users how a decision was reached
Instrument specifically for 'quietly stuck' patterns like no-progress loops — they're common and easy to miss
The most dangerous failures to your users' trust are the ones that don't look like failures at all

questions.prompt: According to the paper, what is an "agentic delegation failure"?
options: Any case where the agent crashes or throws an error
A case where the agent's process departs from the user's expectations, regardless of whether the end result was technically correct
A failure that only occurs in multi-agent systems
Any failure that a safety red-team can reproduce
questions.explanation: The paper's central reframing is that failure isn't only about wrong outputs — an agent can complete a task successfully and still fail the user if how it got there violates their expectations.

questions.prompt: What did the 73-person user study find about severity and noticeability?
options: They are unrelated — severity has no effect on how easily users notice a failure
More severe failures are easier to notice, since users pay closer attention to high-stakes tasks
More severe failures tend to be harder to notice, while prior experience with a failure type makes it easier to spot
Noticeability only depends on how long the agent ran
questions.explanation: The study found an inverse relationship: failures rated as more severe were also rated as harder to notice in the moment, while having previously seen a given failure type improved detection — a concerning combination for high-stakes agent use.

questions.prompt: Why do the authors highlight "agents running without making progress" as a notable example?
options: Because it's the most severe failure category in the taxonomy
Because it's rare but catastrophic
Because it's common in real usage yet received little prior research attention, and doesn't trip standard crash/error-based evaluation
Because it only happens in multi-agent orchestration systems
questions.explanation: The paper specifically calls this out as a failure that's frequent in the Reddit corpus but under-studied — it doesn't look like a crash or a wrong answer, so standard benchmarks miss it even though users experience it as wasted time and cost.

posts.title: SGLang's Paged Experts: Giant MoE Models on One Consumer GPU
posts.subtitle: A new opt-in paging trick beats CPU offload by up to 30x
posts.summary: SGLang v0.5.23 (Nov 2, 2026) adds 'Paged Experts,' an opt-in feature that lets mixture-of-experts models bigger than a GPU's VRAM run on a single consumer card — up to 30x faster than the previous CPU-offload fallback. The same release adds fused low-latency decode kernels, Google TPU7x support, and LoRA serving on quantized MoE models.

slides.title: A Model Too Big for Your GPU. One Flag Fixes the Math.
slides.body: Mixture-of-experts models can have far more total parameters than any single consumer GPU's VRAM. SGLang's new release makes that gap survivable without a server rack.
bullets: SGLang v0.5.23 — released Nov 2, 2026
1,007 PRs, 257 contributors in this release alone

slides.title: MoE Models Outgrow Consumer GPUs by Design
slides.body: A mixture-of-experts model only activates a fraction of its experts per token, but all the experts still have to live somewhere in memory to be available.
bullets: Total parameter count (all experts combined) routinely exceeds a 16GB or 24GB consumer card's VRAM
The prior fallback, SGLang's --cpu-offload-gb flag, keeps unused experts in CPU RAM and streams them over PCIe on demand
PCIe bandwidth is the bottleneck: swapping experts in and out on every forward pass is slow enough to make the model impractical for real use

slides.title: Paged Experts: Treat Expert Weights Like OS Virtual Memory
slides.body: The new opt-in feature (PRs #42557 and #45787) pages expert weights in and out of GPU memory the way an operating system pages memory to disk — only moving what's needed, when it's needed.
bullets: Lets MoE models whose total weights don't fit in VRAM run on a single consumer GPU
Reported gain: 12x–30x faster single-stream decode versus --cpu-offload-gb on a 16GB card
Supports quantized experts out of the box: AWQ, compressed-tensors, MXFP4, NVFP4, W8A8, and block-INT8
Opt-in — existing serving setups are unaffected unless explicitly enabled

slides.title: The Rest of v0.5.23: Not Just Paging
slides.body: Paged Experts is the headline, but the release ships several other serving-focused upgrades in the same cut.
bullets: Megakernel (NVIDIA) and monokernel (AMD) fused decode kernels: up to 44% faster single-user decode on GB300, up to 75% faster on MI350X for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash
SGLang-TorchTPU: a new PyTorch-native plugin adding Google TPU7x support
A new opt-in LoRA engine (PR #45892) serves LoRA adapters on quantized MoE models — specifically FP8 and NVFP4 experts

slides.title: Paged Experts vs. the Old CPU-Offload Path
slides.body: Both approaches solve the same problem — fitting a too-big MoE model on one GPU — but land in very different places on speed.

slides.title: Who This Actually Unlocks
slides.body: Picture a developer with a single RTX 4080 (16GB) who wants to experiment with a large MoE model locally.
bullets: Before: either rent a multi-GPU cluster, or use CPU offload and accept decode speeds too slow for interactive use
Now: enable Paged Experts with a quantized expert format (e.g. NVFP4), and the same model runs on that one card at up to 30x the prior offload speed
This doesn't make the GPU bigger — it makes the parts of the model that don't fit cost much less to borrow back from CPU RAM when needed

slides.title: Where It Falls Short
slides.body: Paged Experts is a real unlock, not a replacement for having enough VRAM.
bullets: Still opt-in and newly shipped — expect rough edges relative to SGLang's mature all-on-GPU path
Latency remains higher than serving a model that fits entirely in VRAM; paging still costs real PCIe transfer time, just much less of it
Built for single-stream/low-concurrency use — it is not positioned as a high-throughput multi-request production serving mode
Benefits depend on quantized expert formats being available for your specific model

slides.title: What to Remember
slides.body: SGLang v0.5.23 turns 'this MoE model is too big for my GPU' into a solvable problem for local and small-scale use.
bullets: Paged Experts: 12x–30x faster than CPU offload for oversized MoE models on a single consumer GPU, opt-in
Ships alongside megakernel/monokernel decode speedups, TPU7x support, and quantized-MoE LoRA serving
Best fit: single-user local experimentation on consumer hardware, not high-concurrency production serving
Released Nov 2, 2026 as part of a 1,007-PR release cycle

questions.prompt: What problem does SGLang's 'Paged Experts' feature solve?
options: It speeds up training of mixture-of-experts models
It lets MoE models whose total weight size exceeds a single GPU's VRAM run on that one consumer GPU
It reduces the number of experts a model needs at inference time
It compresses model weights permanently to a smaller file size
questions.explanation: Paged Experts pages expert weights between GPU and CPU memory on demand, similar to OS virtual memory, so a MoE model larger than the GPU's VRAM can still run on that single card.

questions.prompt: How does Paged Experts compare to the prior --cpu-offload-gb approach, per the release notes?
options: It's slower but uses less memory
It's roughly equivalent in speed but easier to configure
It reports 12x-30x faster single-stream decode on a 16GB card
It removes the need for any CPU memory at all
questions.explanation: The release notes report a 12x to 30x single-stream decode speedup over the previous --cpu-offload-gb flag on a 16GB GPU, since Paged Experts moves data more efficiently than the older offload path.

questions.prompt: What is Paged Experts NOT well suited for, according to its own limitations?
options: Running on consumer-grade GPUs
Quantized expert formats like NVFP4
High-throughput, high-concurrency production serving with many simultaneous requests
Single-user local experimentation
questions.explanation: The feature is described as built for single-stream, low-concurrency use — it unlocks running oversized models at all, but isn't positioned to replace fully-in-VRAM serving for high-throughput production workloads.

posts.title: vLLM v0.33.0: CUDA 13-Only Builds, Day-0 Model Support
posts.subtitle: A major open-source serving engine drops CUDA 12.9 and ships six new models on release day.
posts.summary: vLLM v0.33.0 (Nov 2) moves its official builds to CUDA 13.0 only, adds day-0 support for six-plus new models, upgrades speculative decoding with a lossy verification mode, and removes three legacy code paths. It's a snapshot of how fast open-source LLM serving infrastructure is turning over.

slides.title: vLLM v0.33.0 Lands With a Hard CUDA Cutover
slides.body: Released Nov 2, this is the third vLLM minor release in a month — and the first to require CUDA 13.0, dropping 12.9 artifacts entirely.

slides.title: Serving Infra Has to Chase Hardware and Models at Once
slides.body: A serving engine used in production has two moving targets: new accelerators (Blackwell, MI355X, GB300) that need bespoke kernels, and a flood of new open models that need day-0 support before anyone can even benchmark them.
bullets: Every new GPU generation (Blackwell, MI355X) needs its own attention/decode kernel to actually see a speedup
Each new model architecture can break existing speculative-decoding drafters built for a different shape
Carrying old CUDA/ROCm targets forever means never fully optimizing for the new ones

slides.title: What v0.33.0 Actually Ships
slides.body: The release bundles a platform bump, hardware-specific decode paths, and speculative-decoding upgrades.
bullets: Platform: upgraded to PyTorch 2.14; release wheels/images now target CUDA 13.0 only — no more CUDA 12.9 artifacts
NVIDIA: opt-in latency-specialized decode on GB300, plus FA4 sparse MLA decode on Blackwell
AMD: default ROCm build moves to ROCm 10.0, with new MonoKernel decode for several MI300X/MI355X models
Speculative decoding: new 'XPress' refiner for block-diffusion drafters, an opt-in lossy verification policy ('FLy'), and a quantized draft lm_head option
Serving API: new /v1/decisions endpoint, late-chunking support on /v1/embeddings, and a watchdog that dumps stack traces from stuck worker processes

slides.title: Three Releases, Three Different Bets
slides.body: Looking at the last month of minor releases shows the project rotating its focus rather than doing everything at once.

rows: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash perf (FlashMLA + NVFP4 KV cache) and fast-restart via weight preloading
Structured-output endpoint (/v1/systemone), low-precision KV cache rollout, Model Runner V2
CUDA 13-only platform cutover, day-0 models, speculative-decoding overhaul

slides.title: What an Upgrade Actually Looks Like
slides.body: A team running inference on a GB300 cluster, serving one of the new day-0 models (e.g. Step-5 Preview), hits two changes at once when they pull v0.33.0.
bullets: Gain: the GB300 latency-specialized decode path and FA4 sparse MLA (Blackwell) can cut per-token latency without any model change
Break: their CUDA 12.9 image no longer exists upstream — the CI pipeline must rebuild against CUDA 13.0 before the upgrade even runs
Break: if they were using Medusa or the MLP speculator for speculative decoding, that code path is gone and must be replaced with a supported drafter

slides.title: Pitfalls Before You Upgrade
slides.body: This is a breaking release, not a drop-in update.
bullets: Confirm your CI/deploy images can build against CUDA 13.0 — 12.9 artifacts are not published for this version
Medusa, the MLP speculator, and the legacy Ray compiled-graph executor are removed outright, not deprecated
AMD fleets on older ROCm should test on ROCm 10.0 before rolling this out — MonoKernel decode is new, not universal across MI-series cards
Treat each minor vLLM release as a potential breaking change: the project ships fast (three minors in a month) and doesn't hold back removals

questions.prompt: What's the key platform change in vLLM v0.33.0?
options: It drops Python 3.10 support
Release wheels/images now target CUDA 13.0 only, with CUDA 12.9 artifacts no longer published
It removes GPU support entirely in favor of CPU inference
It switches from PyTorch to JAX
questions.explanation: v0.33.0 upgrades to PyTorch 2.14 and moves official builds to CUDA 13.0 exclusively — teams still on CUDA 12.9 images need to rebuild before upgrading.

questions.prompt: Which speculative-decoding components does v0.33.0 remove?
options: Draft-model speculative decoding and custom logits processors
The GPU n-gram speculator
Medusa, the MLP speculator, and the legacy Ray compiled-graph executor
The LiLiCorr drafter
questions.explanation: Those three were marked as breaking removals in v0.33.0's release notes — code relying on them needs to migrate to a currently-supported drafter.

questions.prompt: What new capability did v0.33.0 add to vLLM's hardware support?
options: FA4 sparse MLA decode on Blackwell and MonoKernel decode on MI300X/MI355X under ROCm 10.0
Support for TPU v6
A fallback to CPU-only inference when no GPU is detected
Native support for quantum accelerators
questions.explanation: The release adds hardware-specific decode paths for both NVIDIA Blackwell (FA4 sparse MLA) and AMD's newest MI-series cards under the ROCm 10.0 default build.

posts.title: Chunking: The RAG Decision Everyone Underrates
posts.subtitle: How you cut a document up matters more than which embedding model you pick.
posts.summary: Chunking — how a document gets split before embedding — silently caps RAG recall long before the LLM sees anything. Fixed-size, recursive, semantic, and sentence-window chunking each trade off recall, cost, and complexity differently, and picking wrong hurts more than any embedding-model swap.

slides.title: The Chunk Boundary You Draw Decides What's Findable
slides.body: Split a document wrong and no embedding model, however good, can recover the signal you just threw away.

slides.title: One Vector Has to Represent a Whole Chunk
slides.body: Embedding models compress a chunk into a single fixed-size vector. Cram in too much and distinct ideas average into mush; cut it too small and you lose the context that made the passage answer the question.
bullets: A 2,000-token chunk covering five subtopics embeds as a blurry average — a query about any one subtopic matches weakly
A 50-token chunk can be too thin to retrieve at all if the matching keywords and the actual answer sit in different chunks
Most production systems land chunk size somewhere in the 200–500 token range, not because it's magic, but because it's small enough to stay topically coherent and large enough to carry real context

slides.title: Four Chunking Strategies, Four Different Bets
slides.body: Each strategy decides where to cut based on different information about the document.
bullets: Fixed-size with overlap: split every N tokens, overlap ~10–20% so an idea split across a boundary still appears whole in at least one chunk
Recursive/structure-aware: split on paragraph breaks first, then sentences, then words only as a last resort — keeps natural units intact
Semantic chunking: embed sentences, then cut where embedding similarity between consecutive sentences drops sharply — follows topic shifts, not token counts
Sentence-window: retrieve on a small chunk (1–2 sentences) for precision, but send the LLM a wider window around it for context — decouples what you match on from what you feed the model

slides.title: Picking a Strategy by What You're Optimizing For

rows: Markdown, code docs, anything with real structure
Long docs that wander across subtopics
Precise fact lookup where the exact sentence matters

slides.title: Same Pipeline, Two Documents, Two Right Answers
slides.body: A 40-page API reference and a customer-support call transcript don't want the same chunker.
bullets: API reference: recursive/structure-aware chunking that respects headers and code blocks — splitting a code sample mid-block makes it useless even if the surrounding prose is intact
Support transcript: sentence-window chunking — a customer's one-line complaint is the retrieval target, but the agent's resolution two turns later is what the LLM actually needs to answer with
Using fixed-size chunking on either would occasionally slice a code block in half or separate a question from its answer purely by token-count coincidence

slides.title: Where Chunking Goes Wrong
bullets: Overlap set too high (>30%) bloats the index and returns near-duplicate chunks that crowd out genuinely different results
Fixed-size chunking with no structural awareness will split tables, code blocks, and numbered steps mid-way — the chunk retrieves but reads as nonsense
Semantic chunking isn't free: it costs an embedding call per sentence at ingest time, which matters at large corpus scale
There's no universal best chunk size — tune it against your own retrieval eval (recall@k), not a blog post's default

questions.prompt: Why does cramming a 2,000-token chunk covering five subtopics into one embedding hurt retrieval?
options: Embedding models can't process chunks that long
The single vector ends up as a blurry average of all five subtopics, so a query about any one of them matches weakly
It makes the vector database run out of storage
It triggers a token-limit error at query time
questions.explanation: A chunk's embedding is one fixed-size vector — the more unrelated content it has to represent, the less precisely it represents any single part of it.

questions.prompt: What does sentence-window chunking decouple?
options: The embedding model from the vector database
What you match on (a small, precise unit) from what you feed the LLM (a wider context window around it)
Training data from inference data
The chunk size from the overlap percentage
questions.explanation: Sentence-window retrieval matches on a narrow 1–2 sentence unit for precision, then expands to surrounding sentences only after retrieval, giving the LLM enough context to actually answer.

questions.prompt: What's the main downside of semantic chunking?
options: It can't handle markdown or code
It requires an embedding call per sentence at ingest time, adding real cost at corpus scale
It only works with one specific embedding model
It always produces chunks larger than fixed-size chunking
questions.explanation: Semantic chunking decides boundaries by comparing sentence-level embeddings, which means extra embedding calls during ingestion — a real cost tradeoff against its better topic coherence.

posts.title: TokenEconomizer: Trimming Coding Agent Costs by 31%
posts.subtitle: A black-box plugin that prunes stale tools and caches lessons learned — no model changes required.
posts.summary: TokenEconomizer sits between a coding agent and its model, pruning unused tools and caching repo-specific lessons across sessions. On SWE-Bench it cut cost 18-31% across five agent-model combinations while mostly holding or improving task success — proof that a lot of agent spend is redundant context, not reasoning.

slides.title: Every Agent Session Starts From Zero
slides.body: Claude Code, Codex, and Copilot CLI all re-send the same tool schemas and relearn the same repo quirks on every single run — and every token costs money.

slides.title: Tool Definitions Alone Can Cost More Than the Task
bullets: Every system prompt reloads the full set of tool schemas, whether the agent needs them or not
A coding agent might carry 20+ tools for a task that only ever touches three of them
Repeated across hundreds of sessions on the same repo, that's pure waste — and it compounds on every single turn

slides.title: Three Mechanisms, Zero Changes to the Model
bullets: Micro-skills: repo facts (build command, test quirks) get written down once confirmed across 3 sessions, then stated upfront instead of rediscovered
Tool pruning: a tool unused for 10 prompts across 2+ sessions (or 5 sessions of any length) drops out of the schema — one command restores it
Failure-loop intervention: a judge model watches for an agent stuck repeating the same failed move and injects a redirect, without ever stopping the turn itself

slides.title: 18-31% Cheaper, Mostly Without Losing Accuracy
bullets: Measured on SWE-Bench across 30 repository x agent-model combinations
Cheaper in all 30 cells; Pass@1 (task success) rose in 4 of the 5 agent-model combinations

slides.title: A Repo the Agent Has Seen Before
slides.body: On session one, the agent discovers that `make test` needs ENV=ci set or it hangs. By session four, TokenEconomizer has promoted that into a micro-skill: the agent is told upfront, skipping the trial-and-error loop that burned tokens in sessions one through three.

slides.title: Where the Savings Can Backfire
bullets: Cold-start repos see no benefit yet — micro-skills only kick in after 3 confirmed sessions
A wrongly-pruned tool mid-task still forces an extra round-trip to restore it
The judge model that detects failure loops adds its own token cost — net savings assume it fires rarely
One of five combinations (Copilot CLI + Sonnet 5) saw Pass@1 drop by 1.0 point — cheaper isn't always strictly better

slides.title: A Black Box Around the Agent, Not Inside It
bullets: Sits between the agent harness and the model API, rewriting the context window — never touches model weights
Works today with Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot CLI, and Pi; opencode and Cursor Agent support is experimental
Open source under Apache 2.0, published by Microsoft Research

slides.title: The Takeaway
bullets: Most coding-agent cost isn't the reasoning step — it's redundant context: tool schemas and rediscovered repo facts
A thin caching/pruning layer outside the model cut cost 18-31% with no fine-tuning in these measurements
The pattern generalizes: any agent harness re-sending static context on every call is a candidate for the same trick

posts.title: Mamba: Sequence Modeling Without Quadratic Attention
posts.subtitle: A selective state-space layer that scales linearly with sequence length — no attention matrix required.
posts.summary: Mamba replaces self-attention with a selective state-space recurrence: a fixed-size hidden state updated in parallel, giving linear-time compute and constant memory per generated token. It trades away some of attention's exact recall for dramatically cheaper long-context processing, which is why most deployed long-context models hybridize the two rather than picking one.

slides.title: Attention Isn't the Only Way to Model a Sequence
slides.body: Transformers compare every token to every other token. Mamba instead carries a compressed running state forward, token by token — closer to how an RNN works, but fast enough to compete with attention.

slides.title: Attention's Bill Grows Quadratically
bullets: Self-attention computes an N x N score matrix — double the sequence length, quadruple the compute and memory
The KV cache that stores past keys/values grows linearly with every generated token, eating GPU memory on long outputs
Recurrent nets (RNNs/LSTMs) scale linearly but train slowly — they can't be parallelized across time the way attention can

slides.title: A Selective State That Updates in Parallel
bullets: Mamba keeps a fixed-size hidden state per layer and updates it with a linear recurrence — cost per token is constant, not growing with context
The 'selective' part: input-dependent gating lets the model decide, per token, how much of the past state to keep vs. overwrite — plain state-space models like S4 can't do this
A hardware-aware parallel scan algorithm computes the recurrence across the whole sequence at once on GPU, instead of looping token by token

slides.title: Linear Time, Constant Memory Per Step
A 200-Page Document, Summarized Token by Token
slides.body: Feed a 200-page contract through a Transformer and the attention matrix needs memory proportional to the square of the token count — long documents force chunking or truncation. A Mamba-based model instead walks through the contract once, continuously compressing everything read so far into a fixed-size state, then generates a summary with no growing cache.

slides.title: Where Mamba Struggles
bullets: Exact retrieval is weaker: 'what was the 3rd number mentioned on page 40?' is easy for attention's direct lookups, hard for a compressed state that may have overwritten it
Pure state-space models lag transformers on in-context learning and copying tasks in published benchmarks
Most production systems hedge with hybrids — architectures like Jamba interleave Mamba layers with a few attention layers to keep precise recall where it matters

slides.title: Where It Fits Today
bullets: Best suited for very long contexts where attention's memory cost is the bottleneck: genomics, audio, long documents
Hybrid architectures (Mamba plus sparse attention) are more common in deployed models than pure state-space models
Same training recipes (next-token prediction, RLHF/DPO) apply — it's a drop-in architecture change, not a new training paradigm

slides.title: The Takeaway
bullets: Mamba trades attention's exact, quadratic lookups for a compressed, linear-time running state
That trade wins decisively on raw long-context throughput and memory, and loses on precise recall
The practical answer for most production models isn't 'replace attention' — it's a hybrid that uses each where it's strongest

questions.prompt: Why does a Transformer's self-attention get expensive on long sequences?
options: It needs more training data
The attention score matrix grows quadratically with sequence length
It requires more GPUs for identical throughput
It can only process one token at a time
questions.explanation: Every token attends to every other token, so an N-token sequence needs an N x N score matrix — compute and memory both grow with the square of N.

questions.prompt: What makes Mamba 'selective' compared to earlier state-space models like S4?
options: It uses attention internally
Its state update is input-dependent, letting the model decide what to keep or discard per token
It only processes selected tokens and skips the rest
It requires manual feature selection before training
questions.explanation: Plain state-space models use fixed, input-independent dynamics. Mamba's gating lets the update depend on the current token, which is what lets it compete with attention on language tasks.

questions.prompt: Why do many production long-context models combine Mamba layers with some attention layers instead of using Mamba alone?
options: Pure Mamba models are too slow to train
Attention is required for the model to be differentiable
Mamba's compressed state is weaker at exact recall, so a few attention layers recover precise lookups
Mamba can't run on GPUs
questions.explanation: Mamba's fixed-size state can't perfectly preserve every past token the way attention's direct lookups can, so hybrids like Jamba keep a few attention layers for tasks that need exact recall.

posts.title: Quantization: Shrinking LLMs by Rounding Their Weights
posts.subtitle: Store weights in 4 or 8 bits instead of 16, and a 70B model suddenly fits on one GPU.
posts.summary: Quantization compresses a trained model's weights from 16-bit floats down to 8-bit or 4-bit integers, cutting memory and bandwidth needs by 2-4x with only a small, often-recoverable quality cost. Modern post-training methods like GPTQ and AWQ make this practical without retraining the whole model, which is why it's the default trick for running big LLMs on smaller hardware.

slides.title: Why a 70B Model Doesn't Need 32 Bits Per Weight
slides.body: Every weight in a neural network is just a number. Quantization asks: do we really need 16 or 32 bits of precision to store it, or would 8 or even 4 bits do almost as well?
bullets: A 70B-parameter model in FP16 needs ~140GB of memory just for weights
Quantized to INT4, the same weights fit in roughly 35-40GB — small enough for a single high-end consumer GPU
The technique is central to 'inference optimization': it shrinks cost and latency, not training time

slides.title: The Memory Wall: Compute Is Cheap, Moving Weights Isn't
slides.body: Modern GPUs can do trillions of operations per second, but inference is often bottlenecked by moving weights from GPU memory to the compute cores, not by the math itself.
bullets: Autoregressive decoding generates one token at a time, re-reading the entire weight matrix from memory for every single token
Smaller weights mean less data to move per step, which directly speeds up token generation on memory-bandwidth-bound hardware
Big models also need more GPUs just to hold weights in VRAM, before a single request is served — fewer GPUs needed means lower cost per request

slides.title: From Floats to Integers: Scale, Round, Store
slides.body: At its core, quantization maps a range of floating-point values to a small set of integers using a scale factor (and sometimes a zero-point offset), then reverses the mapping at compute time.
bullets: Per-tensor quantization uses one scale for a whole weight matrix; per-channel or per-group quantization uses many smaller scales for better accuracy
Post-training quantization (PTQ) — methods like GPTQ and AWQ — quantizes an already-trained model using a small calibration dataset, no retraining required
GPTQ quantizes weights layer-by-layer, adjusting remaining unquantized weights to compensate for the error just introduced — this is what keeps 4-bit models usably accurate
AWQ instead identifies the small fraction of 'salient' weight channels most sensitive to error (tied to large activation magnitudes) and protects those specifically

slides.title: Precision Formats: The Memory/Quality Tradeoff
slides.body: Roughly how precision choice affects a model's footprint and typical quality impact (actual numbers vary by model and method):
bullets: FP16 is the common training/serving baseline; INT8 is close to a free lunch for most models
INT4 with a good calibration method (GPTQ/AWQ) usually stays close to FP16 quality on most benchmarks, but the gap widens on tasks needing precise numerical or multi-step reasoning

slides.title: Worked Example: Fitting a 70B Model on One GPU
slides.body: A team wants to self-host a 70B open-weight model for internal tooling but only has a single 48GB GPU.
bullets: In FP16, the weights alone (~140GB) can't even load — they'd need 4+ high-memory GPUs just for storage
Quantized to 4-bit with AWQ, the weights shrink to ~35-40GB, leaving headroom for the KV cache and fitting on one card
They run a quick calibration pass (a few hundred representative prompts) so the quantizer knows which activation channels matter most before compressing
Result: one GPU serves the model at a modest quality cost, instead of needing a multi-GPU cluster for the same workload

slides.title: Pitfalls and When Not to Quantize
slides.body: Quantization isn't free, and pushing it too far or applying it carelessly can quietly break a model in ways standard benchmarks miss.
bullets: Outlier activations (a small number of unusually large values) are the main source of quantization error — methods that ignore them degrade badly at low bit-widths
Aggregate benchmark scores can look fine while specific capabilities (precise arithmetic, long-context recall, rare-but-critical edge cases) quietly degrade
Calibration data that doesn't match real traffic (e.g. calibrating on English text, deploying on code) can quantize the wrong channels well and the wrong ones poorly
Below ~3-4 bits, quality loss tends to grow sharply — most production deployments stop at INT4 or INT8 rather than going lower
Hardware/kernel support matters: a quantization format is only as fast as the inference engine's kernels for it — not every format is accelerated on every GPU

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.body: Quantization trades a small, often-manageable amount of accuracy for large, reliable savings in memory and serving cost.
bullets: INT8 is close to free; INT4 needs a good calibration method (GPTQ, AWQ) to stay accurate
The real bottleneck it solves is memory bandwidth during token-by-token decoding, not raw compute
Always validate on your actual task distribution, not just aggregate benchmarks — quality loss can be uneven across capabilities
It's a serving-time optimization, complementary to (not a replacement for) techniques like KV-cache compression or speculative decoding

questions.prompt: What is the primary bottleneck that weight quantization addresses during LLM inference?
options: The number of floating-point operations the GPU can perform per second
Memory bandwidth — moving weights from memory to compute cores for every generated token
The size of the training dataset used to pretrain the model
Network latency between the client and the server
questions.explanation: Autoregressive decoding re-reads the full weight matrix for every token generated, so inference is often memory-bandwidth-bound, not compute-bound. Smaller (quantized) weights mean less data to move per step, which speeds up generation.

questions.prompt: Why do methods like GPTQ and AWQ use a small calibration dataset instead of just rounding every weight independently?
options: To retrain the entire model from scratch on new data
To measure which weights/channels matter most for real outputs, so errors can be minimized or compensated for where it counts
To generate synthetic training data for the next model version
Calibration data is required by law for releasing open-weight models
questions.explanation: Naive rounding treats every weight equally, but errors aren't equally costly. GPTQ compensates remaining weights for error introduced earlier in the same layer; AWQ protects the specific channels tied to large activations. Both use a small calibration set to find what actually matters — neither retrains the model.

questions.prompt: A team quantizes a model to INT4 and sees nearly identical scores on standard benchmarks, but users report the model suddenly makes more arithmetic mistakes. What's the most likely explanation?
options: INT4 quantization always improves reasoning performance
The benchmark suite doesn't cover the capability that degraded, even though aggregate scores look fine
This is impossible — quantization cannot affect specific capabilities
The GPU hardware is defective
questions.explanation: Quality loss from quantization is often uneven: broad benchmarks can look stable while precise, low-tolerance capabilities like multi-step arithmetic degrade more than average. This is why the pitfalls slide stresses validating on your actual task distribution, not just aggregate scores.

posts.title: Claude Haiku 5.5: 75% Cheaper, Built for Agent Fleets
posts.subtitle: Anthropic's smallest model gets an effort dial, a steep price cut, and a job as every bigger model's subagent.
posts.summary: Anthropic's Claude Haiku 5.5 is its fastest and cheapest model yet, costing roughly 75% less than Haiku 4.5 while adding its first adjustable effort setting and a role as a subagent for Opus and Sonnet on coding tasks. It jumps dramatically over Haiku 4.5 on every reported benchmark but still trails Sonnet 5.5 badly on hard reasoning.

slides.title: A Small Model Built to Run at Fleet Scale
slides.body: Released October 7, 2026 as the fifth model in the Claude 5.5 family, after Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5.
bullets: About 75% cheaper than Haiku 4.5 on average: $0.10/M input, $0.50/M output tokens (prompts up to 100K)
Anthropic's fastest model at standard speed, meant for summaries, classification, and live support
First Haiku model with an adjustable effort dial, from Low to Max

slides.title: Why a Cheaper, Dumber Model Is the Real Scaling Bottleneck
slides.body: Most production AI traffic isn't a hard reasoning question — it's summarization, classification, and routine subagent calls repeated millions of times, where token price matters more than ceiling intelligence.
bullets: Sonnet 5.5 costs 20x more per input token than Haiku 5.5 ($2.00 vs $0.10 per 1M, ≤100K context)
Agent systems increasingly delegate narrow subtasks to a cheap model instead of calling the flagship for everything

bullets: Effort levels: Low, Medium, High, Xhigh, Max — same model, different latency/quality tradeoff per call
